headline: Film: Homage to Garcia Lorca:In Museum Series
abstract: "TO AN UNKNOWN GOD" ("A un Dios Desconocido"), the second feature film by Jaime Chavarri, the Spanish director, is a handsome, densely packed, evocative movie that makes a lot of rather stern demands upon anyone who sees it. It's the sort of thing one should prepare for, like an uncut "Hamlet," a full-length "Die Meistersinger" or a "Blood Wedding" in Spanish.The film, which will be shown at the Museum of Modern Art today at 8:30 P.M. and on Monday at 6 P.M., is one of three that today begins the annual New Directors/New Films series at the museum. The series is jointly presented by the museum's department of film and the Lincoln Center Film Society.Like the recent films of Carlos Saura and Victor Erice, "To an Unknown God" recalls the legacy of nearly 40 years of the Franco dictatorship but it does this in terms that are so special, so private, that one attends the film as if it were a meeting of cabalists. The movie is full of secret signs and mysterious associations. Over it all hangs the ghost of Federico Garcia Lorca, the Spanish poet and playwright who was murdered in 1936 by the Falangists who despised his homosexuality as much as his left-wing politics.Though most of the film is the contemporary memoir of a middle-aged, homosexual magician named José (Hector Alterio), the film opens in Granada in 1936 when José as a small boy, was seduced by an older boy who was living in the elegant old house where Garcia Lorca's murder, this opening sec-unfamiliar with the circumstances of Garcia Lorca's murder, this opening section makes no sense whatsoever. As it is, one never is exactly sure who José's young male lover is, or what his connection is to the famous guest, who is seen once in a long, shot, much as Christ is sometimes glimpsed in Biblical epics.José appears to be a successful magician, at least in bookings, but his life is fastidiously lonely. Though his somewhat younger lover, Miguel (Javier Elorriaga), a worker on behalf of radical causes, is open-hearted and generous, José devotes himself to the memory of his lost youth. At one point he returns to Granada for a reconciliation with a woman who, like José is obsessed by the memory of Garcia Lorca as well as by the memory of the boy, now dead, whom they both loved.For some peculiar reason, English subtitles, which adequately translate most of the film's Spanish dialogue, are denied us in two key sequences in which José as he's going to bed, plays a tape containing (I think) José himself speaking Garcia Lorca's poetry. Perhaps Mr. Chavarri thinks it would be sacrilege to translate the poet's lines as mere subtitles. In any case we are denied key information and must make out as best we can by recognizing, on the tape, references to "Valt Vitmann" and the Spanish words meaning "sleep," "dream" and "death."Because of its Spanish origin, "To an Unknown God" has astonished a number of European critics for its frank, unhysterical treatment of homosexuality, but the truth is that Mr. Chavarri's particular preoccupations result in a movie that seems as self-interested, even arrogant, as poor, lonely José. "To an Unknown God" is lovely to look at, highly cultivated and poised, and very, very difficult to get to know.

headline: Redemption and Resurrection Are Themes of 'Barocco' Film
abstract: Behind the opening credits of "Barocco," André Téchiné's second feature to be shown in New York (his first was "French Provincial"), we see a series of distorted close-ups of such exotic fauna as crocodiles, giant snakes and horned lizards so ancient they might have witnessed creation—images designed to make the flesh crawl with primal fears.It's something of a disappointment, then, that when the film begins, we are in a neon-bright, busy, commercial European city. It's actually Amsterdam, though the film never specifically says so, which is one of the smaller affectations of this would-be thriller that cares less about the fundamental mechanics of murder, blackmail and physical intimidation than it does about such weighty subjects as redemption and resurrection."Barocco" will be shown at the Museum of Modern Art tonight at 11 in the annual New Directors/New Films series, and again tomorrow evening at 6.Mr. Téchiné, who was born in 1943, belongs to a second generation of French film critics associated with Cahiers du Cinema who followed François Truffaut, Claude Chabrol and others from criticism into film-making. On the basis of both "French Provincial," which was about nothing less than the rise and fall of the French bourgeoisie, and now "Barocco," Mr. Téchiné remains more of a theorist than an artist.His films have a way of starting off very well and then slowly congealing into stiff, intellectualized attitudes that have less to do with art than with its interpretation. Only Mr. Chabrol, at the top of his form, and Wim Wenders, in his recent "The American Friend," successfully manage to fuse the two disciplines."Barocco" means to be baroque, but it's about as baroque as a pedant's laundry list. It's a schematic tale of murder and blackmail during a municipal election. Its focal point is a nice dumb-lug of a boxer, played by Gérard Dépardieu, who is paid a handsome fee to say he had a homosexual affair with one of the candidates, and the boxer's girl, played by Isabelle Adjani, who originally persuaded the boxer to take the bribe so that they could flee to more exotic climates.Something goes wrong, however, and the boxer is murdered and Miss Adjani finds herself falling in love with the hood who murdered her lover. This is easy to understand. The hood is also played by Mr. Dépardieu, though "Barocco" would have us believe that the girl's love redeems the murderer and, in effect, resurrects him. Nonsense. The miracle is in the casting."Barocco" is a very classy looking movie, with lots of fancy camerawork in lots of fancy, ultramodern settings. In addition to Mr. Dépardieu and Miss Adjani, the cast includes such superior performers as Marie-France Pisier, who has some funny moments as a hooker, Jean-Claude Briarly, and Claude Brasseur. They are most attractive, lively people, but their material is dead.

headline: Film: Turks in Sweden:Stockholm Saga
abstract: "THE BUS," a Turkish-Swiss coproduction filmed mostly in Sweden, is as sincere as a public-service ad on behalf of clean air but somewhat less engrossing. The film, which was written, directed and produced by Bay Okan, a leading Turkish actor who also stars in it, will be shown in the New Directors/New Films series at the Museum of Modern Art today at 6 P.M. and again on Friday at 9:30 P.M."The Bus" is about a group of Turkish workers who are swindled by a compatriot who smuggles them into Sweden, takes their money and then leaves them sitting in their bus in the middle of Stockholm.For three days they remain in the bus, the curtains drawn, suspecting the worst. At night they sneak out to go to a nearby lavatory, forage for food and explore the cruel city.One fellow is picked up by a homosexual and goes mad, as if that were the natural order of events. All are hungry and not one of them is more articulate than a Labrador retriever. Though it's a sad story, Mr. Okan never makes it seem especially moving, maybe because his pretentions as a film artist get in his way.He has a fondness for starting scenes by having the image swim into focus, as if someone were awakening with a hangover. The camera is fascinated by the usual oddities and ugliness of urban living and by horizontal panshots, which make you feel as if your eyeballs had come loose. Mr. Okan himself plays the immigrant worker who goes to spectacular pieces. The only other easily indentifiable role, that of the swindling bus driver, a fellow who in turn is swindled himself, played by Ogur Arlas. The performances are not great.The film is meant, I suspect, to ???are so dense, so naiïve and so faceless???tion of the innocent, but the workers are so dense, so naiïve and so faceless that it seems more to be an indictment of native ignorance.

headline: Screen: Growing Up German at the Modern:Tyranny and Growth
abstract: THE title character in both of these films is a dark-haired youth of 15, slim, silent, finished with school, seemingly not very bright, and suffering under a father's tyrannical rule.In "Paule Paulander," the father is a pig farmer; in "The Main Actor," the proprietor of a rural junkyard. Reinhard Hauff, the director, in other words, seems to have scoured West Germany for unlovely settings, not picturesque villages and valleys or bright and bustling towns. The country is flat, the people coarse, the color photography dim. In short, we are mired in the "realism" into which young film makers are apt to stumble while seeking a shortcut to Parnassus. Or in this instance to the Museum of Modern Art, where the two films will be shown at 6 P.M. today and at 8:30 P.M. tomorrow as part of the New Directors/New Films series.The climax of "Paule Paulander" occurs when an outbreak of swine fever—not to be confused with swine flu—ruins the father and brings on an emotional breakdown. The youth knocks away the rifle that his father is threatening him with and clubs him briskly with a shovel. Leaving the stubborn old fellow moaning on a pile of dying piglets, he abandons the acres that his family has tilled for 300 years to seek his fortunes in the big city.In "The Main Actor" the youth is recruited to play the starring role in a film within a film, an unsparing quasi-documentary look into the horrors of rural life, as seen from the perspective of the film's director, who seems to be a socialist of some sort and it is hinted, a homosexual.Tired of dismantling old Volkswagens, encouraged by his father's kicks and cuffs, this youth abandons the junkyard. He follows the director to what may be the same city, possibly Cologne, where he turns out to be no happier.Mr. Hauff has made the mistake of stating his intentions in a credo distributed at the screening of the films instead of fulfilling them on the screen. For artistic ideological reasons that he fails to make entirely clear in the statement, he has amateur actors in "Paule Paulander" and professionals in "The Main Actor." Both perform at about the same level of plodding inadequacy, with the edge, perhaps, going to the amateurs.

headline: Headliners
abstract: Sex and crime are a volatile combination, especially in politics. For years, Jeremy Thorpe, former leader of Britain's Liberal Party, has been dogged by allegations that he had a homosexual relationship with Norman Scott, a onetime male model. The second ingredient for a first‐rate political scandal was added last week: Mr. Thorpe and three political friends were charged with conspiring to murder Mr. Scott, a crime for which Mr. Thorpe could be sentenced to life imprisonment. The homosexual insinuations, which he has consistently denied, forced Mr. Thorpe to resign the Liberal leadership in May 1976, but he held on to a seat in Parliament and was widely respected for his statesmanship. A witty speaker with a gift for mimickry, he was sometimes called “the last of the Edwardians” because of his manner but also for his attire that often included a homburg, waistcoat and heavy watch chain. Now his parliamentary career, and the Liberal Party's dwindling fortunes along with it, are greater jeopardy.

headline: Headliners
abstract: Perhaps because public and private scandals in Britain are usually wrapped in a blanket of propriety and strict libel laws, British political misdeeds, like British murders, tend to appear unusually titillating. Such was the case last week when Jeremy Thorpe, once leader of the Liberal Party, went before a magistrates court to determine if he must stand trial in conspiracy to murder Norman Scott, a former male model who claims to have once been his lover. Mr. Thorpe is accused of having paid $20,000 in 1975 to have Mr. Scott killed, after trying to persuade political associates to do the job. According to prosecution witnesses, Mr. Scott had for many years been threatening to reveal a homosexual relationship with the Liberal leader, and Mr. Thorpe was desperate to get rid him. The murder plot reportedly went awry when the would‐be killer's gun jammed. Mr. Thorpe has denied all charges, well as Mr. Scott's claims. Whether or not the case goes trial, and whatever the verdict in such a trial, Mr Thorpe's once‐brilliant career seems to have been destroyed, and with it the recent hopes of the Liberal Party to return as a significant political force.

headline: Screen: 'Consequence' From West Germany:The Cast
abstract: The first and best part of "The Consequence" is a tender courtship episode, delicately rendered. Martin, a quiet, sad-eyed man of perhaps 30 years old, is imprisoned for having had sex with a 15-year-old boy, and while incarcerated he finds Thomas, the son of one of the prison officials. Thomas (Ernst Hannawald) has the cheek-bones of a female fashion model and the innocent beauty of an angel. And, more to the point, Thomas has a crush on Martin (Jurgen Prochnow) from the moment they meet.Their affair is consummated in the kind of gradual, intimate, not at all sexually explicit love scene one seldom sees between heterosexual couples on the screen any more. The director, Wolfgang Petersen, uses slow, steady camera movements and the natural warmth of his two actors to give this early part of his film — all of which is in black and white — an unusually rosy glow.The rest of "The Consequence," which is a West German contribution to the Museum of Modern Art's New Directors/New Films series, follows Thomas and Martin from one hardship to the next, with society persecuting them at every turn. Martin is denied parole after the prison guards read one of Thomas's love letters. Thomas loses his job for consorting with Martin later on. Thomas winds up in a reform school populated exclusively by goons, including one burly sadist who puts out cigars on the persons of his least-favorite students.Even before the other reform school boys try to force Thomas to have sex with a pimply, feeble-minded girl with thick glasses, Mr. Petersen makes it clear that he favors a stacked deck. Heterosexuality is represented, by this girl and by Thomas's dreadful parents, as the cruelest of fates, and everyone they meet seems determined to harass the lovers. Indeed, until one late scene showing Martin in a homosexual bar, there is little evidence that Switzerland and West Germany, where the film takes place, contain any other homosexuals except these two. Such over-simplifications eventually push the plot over the edge into unabashed melodrama.Still, Mr. Petersen keeps the love story so vivid and simple, in its way, that his more heavy-handed flourishes are easy to ignore. Much of "The Consequence" is sentimental in the nicest sense and genuinely romantic, too. Mr. Petersen demonstrates both technical proficiency and a sensitivity toward the gentler side of his subject.

headline: Screen: 'Nighthawks':Documentary Tone
abstract: "NIGHTHAWKS" is so realistic, or at least so intimately close to its main character, that it has the feeling of a documentary. A London schoolteacher named Jim (Ken Robertson) is seen cruising homosexual bars by night and at work in the daytime, with the camera watching him almost as impartially and guardedly as he seems to be watching the world. The camera works so passively, in fact, that it never establishes anything about Jim directly. And since Jim is quite taciturn, "Nighthawks," which opens at Quad 1 today, sometimes suffers from a dearth of information. But the character is intriguing and well-played, a fellow about whom one would want to know more. And the film, though it's overlong and aimless at times, presents a vivid if mysterious portrait.Certain things can be deduced about Jim from his tendency to choose elusive younger men, from his impenetrable politeness, from the tiny differences between his behavior in homosexual surroundings and his manner at work. He makes no attempt to conceal his homosexuality from his colleagues, nor does he announce it; consequently, a lot of them assume he is heterosexual. There's a very delicate scene in the film between Jim and a woman co-worker who has become his friend, an unhappily married woman who seems to have designs on him. She complains about domestic life with her husband, and Jim talks about his difficulties in living with anyone, too.Jim avoids pronouns for a while, but when he finally refers to a lover as "he," the woman can barely control her disappointment and surprise. But control it she does, because she doesn't want to jeopardize a good friendship. Meanwhile, Jim does the kindest possible thing by staring into his drink to give her time to compose herself.The only other episode that stands out from the film's deliberate pattern of repetition is the moment when a few budding juvenile delinquents in Jim's class taunt him with rumors that he is a homosexual. Jim handles this beautifully, explaining matter-of-factly that the rumors are true and answering a patient "No" each time they ask whether he wears women's dresses or carries a purse. Ron Peck and Paul Hallam, who collaborated on writing, producing and directing the film, almost make the episode look like cinema vérité, and in fact much of the kids' rude catcalling becomes a jumble of noise. So Jim's evenness stands out all the more, as the one constant element in a heated, chaotic scene.There surely must be more to Jim than meets the eye, or than Mr. Hallam and Mr. Peck bother to explain. In the interests of depicting London's homosexual nightlife honestly and accurately, they've short-changed the character to a certain degree, generalizing his experience more than they needed to. They have also sacrificed any shapeliness the film might have had to this same desire for verisimilitude. Still, "Nighthawks" is gentle and believable, and Mr. Robertson gives a performance that's as touching and consistent as the circumstances allow.

There themusicians are, playing along in stately fashion until a banjo seems to predominate, slightly. Then the piano loses control of its pulse, a race to see which instrumentalist can develop the highest blood pressure begins, the whole thing degenerates into the quick hysteria of silent‐movie “hurry” music, and —just when you suppose them exhausted — the musicians recover for a mighty expansion into Handel‐like ecstasy. Very spiritual, finally. And very funny.

headline: The Screen: 'Normande':A Decorative Actress
abstract: THE only reason to see "Normande," Gilles Carle's French-Canadian film that opens today at the Quad Cinema, is to see Carole Laure whom you may have seen earlier in Bertrand Blier's "Get Out Your Handkerchiefs." Miss Laure possibly is a very good actress but at this point in her career she is primarily a decorative object, something to seduce the eye. She is a beautifully molded creature, her limbs finely balanced, with skin so velvety it invites touching.In "Normande" she does get touched from time to time, but not frequently enough to raise this gloomy domestic melodrama to the sunnier level of soft-core pornography. Mostly Miss Laure, in the title role, walks through the movie fully dressed and looking worried, and well she might.Normande works in a drug store and is the sole support of her nutty mother, who thinks of herself as an actress but is actually a long-in-the-tooth porn performer; her younger sister, who has asthma and no love for Normande; her lover, who is unemployed and not breaking his neck looking for work; and an asexual young man who is unhappy because people mistake him for a homosexual.Sharing the house with Normande and her "family," though in different apartments, are a senile old lady who keeps rats as pets, her grandson, who wants to be a musician, and a clean old man who lusts discreetly after Normande.Some suspense is provided by the knowledge that Normande is about to be evicted so that the apartment can be turned into a restaurant. It all becomes too, too much for Normande who retreats into a permanent dream world.The actors aren't bad but the movie is unreliable. Mr. Carle would like us to find something gallant about these eccentrics. Instead, being around them is like being panhandled by bores who ask for pity instead of money.

headline: Screen: Pacino Stars in Friedkin's 'Cruising':Another Country
abstract: "IT'S a world unto itself," says a New York detective early in "Cruising," William Friedkin's muddled melodrama about a particularly bizarre homosexual subculture in New York City. "It's not the mainstream of gay life."That's what the detective says but everywhere the movie goes, it sees nothing but young and not-so-young men who dress as if they were going to a costume ball in a garage for motorcyclists: leather jackets, leather vests, leather jeans, leather boots, leather caps, lots of superfluous chains, everything decorated with the studs that are sequins to members of the fancy s. and m. crowd.When Mr. Friedkin's camera passes through west Greenwich Village on a summer evening, it finds the streets and sidewalks teeming with men, seemingly hundreds of them, all of whom look exactly alike. When the movie goes uptown to seek out a late-night tryst, it finds more people milling around Central Park than you'd see in Times Square on New Year's Eve. According to "Cruising," alien creatures have occupied New York, a city where it's always night for the living dead.Homosexual activist groups, which have been protesting the production of "Cruising" on the grounds that it would present a distorted view of homosexual life, were right. "Cruising" is a homosexual horror film. Even worse is that it's also a faint-hearted one, which is not to say that it's shy. It describes the s. and m. scene with far more leering attention to detail than most people will find necessary.These background images are rudely sensational and ugly, but they are far more plausible than the denatured narrative in the foreground. "Cruising" always seems to be doing its best to avoid admitting what it's about. Perhaps because of the complaints he received during production, Mr. Friedkin has ended up with a movie that's still in a closet.In adapting Gerald Walker's novel for the screen, the director-writer has made crude, sometimes totally confusing changes in the original. This was about a young policeman who goes undercover in search of a killer who's been preying on members of New York's s. and m. community. In the course of the assignment, the cop, finds himself changing, and not for the better. Assuming the identity and habits of a homosexual, he seeks the killer by identifying himself with the killer. Eventually he is the killer — which is the novel's twist.What happens to the film's cop, Steve Burns, is far from clear, though it's not especially ambiguous. The movie is only coherent if one knows Mr. Walker's narrative. In fact, I'm sure, the original story remains in the film, though it's held at such a distance I'd find that difficult to prove.In spite of the gaudiness of the locale, which has been well photographed by James Contner, "Cruising" is a very tepid personal drama. All of Mr. Pacino's best scenes seem to take place offscreen. There's one good moment in the film, when Steve Burns pleads with his boss, played by Paul Sorvino, to take him off the case. He can't take the life, he says desperately, and because he doesn't explain why, we suspect his fears have to do with more than his physical safety.Much of the time "Cruising" simply records the details of the cop's undercover activities — where he lives, how he makes friends, who these people are (professors, designers, actors, busboys, etc.) and, most important, what he sees when he hangs out at the leather bars."Cruising," which opens today at the National and other theaters, is exceptionally unpleasant, not necessarily because of the subject matter, but because it makes no attempt to comprehend it. It just stares.The performances are not bad, but they aren't great either. Mr. Pacino, I suspect, knows what his character is up to even when Mr. Friedkin won't acknowledge it. Mr. Sorvino is once again Old Reliable in a movie that doesn't deserve him. Among the good supporting people are Karen Allen, as the girl Steve Burns leaves behind in the straight world, and Don Scardino, Jay Acovone, Arnaldo Santana and James Remar as some of the people the cop meets in the night. Richard Cox is effective as the cop's prime suspect, a psychotic Columbia music student."Cruising" is not really a murder-mystery. The killer is known early on. It's more on the order of a fictional travelogue, with an ending that is not a resolution of anything but a copout.

headline: Screen: Bill Murray Is Star Of 'Where Buffalo Roam':The Cast Goldenson of ABC Named As Emmy Winner
abstract: Dr. Hunter S. Thompson, the main attraction in "Where the Buffalo Roam," isn't a clear enough character to hang a whole movie on, but he's certainly the life of any party. During the course of the film, Mr. Thompson is seen brightening up a wide variety of occasions as he practices Gonzo journalism, which is something he invented along with that doctoral degree. It certainly takes practice.He takes drugs, then flies an airplane while singing "Lucy in the Sky With Diamonds." He takes more drugs, then shoots his own telecopier machine and takes aim at the telephone whenever it rings. He coaxes a room-service waiter and a maid to set up a very small football game in his hotel room on the day of the Super Bowl, and scores enough touchdowns to splinter all the mirrors. He trades his ticket for the game for a bottle of wine he sees a man drinking on the street. The bottle is in a brown paper bag, but that's fine. Whatever else Mr. Thompson may be, he isn't fussy."Where the Buffalo Roam," which opened yesterday at the Rivoli and stars Bill Murray, includes a number of funny gambits and very little glue. Mr. Murray is clever whenever he is audible — which isn't all the time, because he speaks with a cigarette holder clenched between his teeth, and the film's director, Art Linson, has a way of training the camera away from the speaker, making it difficult to lip-read. But the story rambles desperately, and there are times when the screenplay is barely there. Mr. Thompson's only identifiable quality soon becomes facetiousness, and it wears terribly thin.As a writer for Rolling Stone, which for some reason is called Blast magazine here, Mr. Thompson is seen covering 1968 marijuana trials in San Francisco, the 1972 Super Bowl and the 1972 Presidential campaign, during which he either sees or imagines seeing Richard M. Nixon in a men's room. He is joined in these adventures by a wild-eyed lawyer, played by Peter Boyle; the lawyer, like Mr. Thompson himself, is a figure much more amusingly drawn in Mr. Thompson's writings than he is here. Their carousing goes from funny to flat and back again, lurching unpredictably between extremes. Both Mr. Boyle and Mr. Murray are occasional victims of Mr. Linson's awkward timing, when the film either cuts short laughs or lingers too long on dull material.The score for "Where the Buffalo Roam," by Neil Young, works very well with the film. It includes Motown material, some rock anthems of the late 1960's by Bob Dylan and Jimi Hendrix. It also offers Mr. Young's own approach to "Home on the Range," which is performed here in several haunting versions.The 1979-80 Trustees Award of the National Academy of Television Arts and Sciences has been awarded to Leonard H. Goldenson, chairman and chief executive officer of the American Broadcasting Companies, for "continued distinguished service to television and the public this medium serves."The award, a golden Emmy statue, will be presented at a dinner Tuesday at the Metropolitan Club, on East 60th Street. Among the speakers will be Lord Grade, chairman of the Associated Communications Corporation of England; Elton H. Rule, president of ABC Inc.; Robert J. Wussler, chairman of the academy, and Frederick Pierce, president of ABC Television.Mr. Goldenson joined ABC in the 1950's, when the network merged with United Paramount Theaters, where he was president and chief executive.Recipients of the award, which dates to 1958, have been John F. Kennedy, Bob Hope, Edward R. Murrow, William S. Paley, David Sarnoff, Dr. Frank Stanton, Elmer W. Lower, Donald H. McGannon, Sylvester L. Weaver Jr., and Dr. Peter Goldmark.

headline: Film: 'Gemini' Transferred to Screen:Growing Pains
abstract: THOUGH Richard Benner's "Happy Birthday, Gemini," which opens at the Beekman and other theaters today, is an exceptionally vulgar screen version of Albert Innaurato's hit Broadway play, "Gemini," it at least raises some interesting questions about what passes for realism on our commercial stage.When the play opened three years ago, it was hailed as an uproarious, realistic comedy, the sort that takes place in a reasonable facsimile of an actual place (a lower-middle-class backyard in South Philadelphia) and is about characters who represent nothing more than their own easily recognized personalities. There are differences between people in real life and characters in such plays, but these differences (including a tendency to talk faster than we do and to bear down hard on punch lines) are simply conventions that stand for realism in the theater. Or so we've been led to believe.It isn't until such a play is transferred to the screen — badly — that we can note that the so-called realistic theater has far less to do with realism than it does with fantasy of a not very liberating sort.This is the service performed by Mr. Benner, who both adapted and directed the movie. Having what I assume were nothing but good intentions, Mr. Benner has "opened up" the Innaurato play by moving a lot of the stage action inside the adjoining houses and to other areas in the neighborhood and in downtown Philadelphia. Scenes that are described in the play are dramatized, and characters who are only talked about in the play appear on the screen.Being faithful to the spirit of the stage production, Mr. Benner has also seen fit to preserve a hyperactive style of theatrical performance, which passes for realism on the stage. This not only looks outlandish on the screen, but it also calls fatal attention to the artificial ellipses and exaggerations in what was once a tightly constructed theatrical piece.The result is a disaster. Instead of opening up the Innaurato play, Mr. Benner has effectively dismembered it.This is a film of assorted bits and pieces of characters who originate not in life, but in literature, some of it not of the first freshness.There is the sensitive hero, Francis Geminiani (Alan Rosenberg), a Harvard-educated, opera-loving fellow who, on the eve of his 21st birthday, fears he may be homosexual. Surrounding him are his father (Robert Viharo), a sexually robust, cheek-pinching Sicilian; his father's sharp-talking mistress (Rita Moreno); Francis's two best friends from Harvard (Sarah Holcomb and David Marshall Grant), who are sister and brother and for both of whom Francis has sexual feelings as well as fondness, and the neighborhood's good-time girl (Madeline Kahn), who once played Sadie Thompson in a community theater production of "Rain" and has never forgotten the bright lights.Mr. Benner, who won some acclaim a couple of years ago with the Canadian film "Outrageous," seeks both laughter and tears in Francis's quest for a sexual identity, but finds neither. This is possibly because his direction is so insistent, so pushy, we are never allowed to discover anything for ourselves.If the actors aren't overstressing their lines, the camera is picking up lighting effects that scream the mood we're supposed to be feeling. When all else fails, the soundtrack music takes over like a noisy tour guide who won't shut up.The performances are less terrible, I suspect, than evidence of the director's wrongheadedness. This is apparent in scene after scene in which actors we know and respect from other films perform with an intensity and abandon that cannot be supported by the film that surrounds them here. This is especially true of Miss Kahn, Miss Moreno and Mr. Viharo, who is so good in James Caan's "Hide in Plain Sight."There is one thing to be said in favor of this movie — it isn't likely to steal business from the play, which is now in its fourth year at the Little Theater on 44th Street.

headline: Film 'Fame' Opens, Bubbling With Life:The Long, Long Road
abstract: "FAME" is a jubilant, hugely entertaining movie by a man whose principal directing experience has been the making of commercials, and so it is happier, sexier and a little bit livelier than life. That's no problem, most of the way through; it simply makes "Fame" a film to be enjoyed and taken lightly.The cast is full of glowing newcomers, the score is emphatically upbeat, and the action moves swiftly from character to character, stringing together a lot of subplots in quick succession."Fame" runs into trouble only when it tries to turn wistful. Alan Parker, its director, seems to know everything about making his characters superficially appealing and little about what makes them tick."Fame," which opens today at the Ziegfeld theater, is set at the High School of Performing Arts, where it follows a big, rambling band of characters from their first auditions to graduation day. The audition sequence that begins the film lasts nearly half an hour, and it is spectacular, the best thing "Fame" has to offer. Mr. Parker moves nimbly from one hilariously hair-raising tryout to another, capturing these teenagers' hopes, their silliness, their promise.One girl gets through an acting audition by playing 0. J. Simpson's role as he waited for an elevator in "The Towering Inferno." A boy with an impenetrable New York accent stumbles his way through "Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?" until a weary acting teacher lets him know he's reading the girl's part. A budding composer arrives for a music tryout trailing six pieces of a synthesizer and half his family. Mr. Parker makes all of this deliciously funny, and it races along flawlessly, without missing a beat. The actors aren't uncommonly handsome, but they're all photographed in a style that makes them beautiful, so near it seems you can reach right out and touch them, and bathed in a warm, sunny light. All of "Fame" looks like this; all of a Coca-Cola ad looks like this, too. Whatever "Fame" is selling, it comes in the prettiest, shiniest package the movies have lately seen.Each of Mr. Parker's two previous features, "Bugsy Malone" and "Midnight Express," had its own overpowering sense of style. "Fame," which is by far Mr. Parker's most successful effort, has a comparably impenetrable quality, but the surface is so slick an audience simply glides along as the movie juggles its vignettes. Ralph (Barry Miller) sometimes imagines he's Freddie Prinze. Doris (Maureen Teefy) has a stage mother and a blossoming ambition. Coco (Irene Cara) wants desperately to be a singer, and her talent is so evident she seems well on her way. Leroy (Gene Anthony Ray) is a showstopping dancer and the Don Juan of the classroom, but he may not make it through high school if he does not learn how to read."Fame" whirls past dozens of incidental characters, like the pretty young teacher (Debbie Allen) who nearly swoons at Leroy's audition, or the sterner, more experienced teacher (Anne Meara) whose tart tongue and unflinching manner keep her classes in line. It also frequently breaks into song, into big, noisy, raucous musical interludes to which Mr. Parker brings his utmost flair. These numbers don't always fit the film, but no one seems to care. "Hot Lunch," set in the school cafeteria, is a routine everyone breaks into with no particular spontaneity — even though the film's style has been fairly naturalistic up until this point, and the sight of dozens of dancers executing Louis Falco's choreography utterly ruptures the mood.Eventually, Mr. Parker winds up playing some unnecessary tricks. Coco, who has been seen sitting in a Howard Johnson's in Times Square at the beginning of her freshman year, is approached in the very same restaurant several years later by a bogus Frenchman, who tries to lure her into a pornographic film; she would have to be très stupid to fall for this, but by now the movie is determined to turn sad. Montgomerey (Paul McCrane) announces and bemoans his homosexuality, in a speech so self-pitying it drew hisses at one screening. Lisa (Laura Dean) appears to jump in front of a subway train after a teacher dresses her down — only she doesn't jump, she isn't even thinking of jumping. This is just Mr. Parker's notion of an ironic twist.

headline: REP. LEDERER TO BASE HIS ABSCAM DEFENSE ON ENTRAPMENT ISSUE
abstract: Representative Raymond F. Lederer of Pennsylvania will argue that he is not guilty of bribery and conspiracy charges in his Abscam case because he was a victim of illegal ''entrapment'' by Federal undercover agents, his lawyer said as the Congressman's trial opened yesterday in Federal District Court in Brooklyn.   A defendant is considered a victim of entrapment when law enforcement agents induce him to commit an unlawful act that he was not otherwise disposed to commit.   Mr. Lederer, a 42-year-old Philadelphia Democrat, was not present for the opening day of his trial. He was in Washington, being sworn in for his third term in the House of Representatives as the 97th Congress convened. Of the six House members charged with crimes as a result of the Government's investigation of political corruption, Mr. Lederer was the only one re-elected last fall.

headline: EXCERPTS FROM GUIDELINES ON COVERT OPERATIONS
abstract: Following are excerpts from the guidelines issued today by the Justice Department to govern undercover operations conducted by the Federal Bureau of Investigation:   AUTHORIZATION OF   THE CREATION OF OPPORTUNITIES FOR   ILLEGAL ACTIVITY (1) Entrapment should be scrupulously avoided. Entrapment is the inducement or encouragement of an individual to engage in illegal activity in which he would otherwise not be disposed to engage.   (2) In addition to complying with any legal requirements, before approving an undercover operation involving an invitation to engage in illegal activity, the approving authority should be satisfied that    (a) The corrupt nature of the activity is reasonably clear to potential subjects; (b) There is a reasonable indication that the undercover operation will reveal illegal activities; and (c) The nature of any inducement is not unjustifiable in view of the character of the illegal transaction in which the individual is invited to engage.

headline: GUIDELINES FOR OPERATIONS OF F.B.I. PERMIT BRIBES, BUT BAR ENTRAPMENT
abstract: The Justice Department issued guidelines today under which the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation could, in some cases, authorize undercover agents to offer a bribe to a public official ''even though there is no reasonable indication that that particular individual has engaged, or is engaging'' in a crime.   The guidelines, approved by Attorney General Benjamin R.  Civiletti, were prepared jointly by officials of the bureau and the department. The rules state that ''entrapment should be scrupulously avoided'' in all undercover operations.   The Justice Department, in a statement accompanying the rules, said they were ''significantly more restrictive'' than the law of entrapment or the constitutional principles requiring ''due process of law'' in Federal investigations.

headline: OF ARMS AND MEN
abstract:
In September 1969, I spent evenings for the better part of three weeks deliberately inhaling canvas dust from the sewing tables at a tent factory in Upstate New York. I was merely another college graduate evading the draft. Classified 1-A, and with the Vietnam War still raging, I was attempting to revive a childhood history of bronchial asthma that, I hoped, would keep me safely at home, morally and physically untainted.

I succeeded. Like most of my well-educated, middle-class friends - some of whom went the route of feigned homosexuality, self-induced emaciation or obesity, even flight to Canada -I never entered the armed forces. What it was precisely that most of us ''believed'' - if anything - seems increasingly unclear. Our ''thinking'' was a vague coalescence of fear, self-serving idealism, search for identity, and (in all-too-few cases, I think) genuine opposition to what almost everyone now agrees was a misbegotten, morally indefensible war. For most of us, the logic was hardly Aristotelian: We first decided that we wanted out, then why.

headline: WRITERS ON NEWSPAPERS FOR HOMOSEXUALS SAY THEIR WORK NOW GAINS MORE
abstract: RESPECT By JONATHAN FRIENDLY   Like many reporters, Pat Burke was happy to see that a newspaper in Minneapolis had reprinted the article he wrote for his San Diego paper about murder victims. But he was nowhere near so happy as Don Michaels, who had watched national newspapers and television pursue the story he had developed on homosexuality among the Cuban refugees.    Both Mr. Burke and Mr. Michaels are editors of newspapers directed to a homosexual readership, and they say that the two articles underline the growing significance of the homosexual press in tracking down news of interest to a wider community.   At a two-day convention at the Roosevelt Hotel in New York last week, they and 75 other editors, publishers and advertising representatives discussed some successes - an increase in circulation of their papers and the beginnings of respect from the rest of the journalistic world - and their continuing problems -lack of advertising revenues and generally amateur staffs. They also talked about plans to form a press association that would help them share material and business expertise.

headline: THE NEW 'FIRST BROTHER' GRACIOUSLY ENDURES ROLE
abstract: A resident of this pleasant community north of San Diego stopped at a local inn for a drink the other night and was approached by a stranger who ''talked like the sun sets and rises on Ronald Reagan.''   ''I had had great visions of walking in and having a quiet snort and some relaxation,'' the resident said. ''All this guy wanted to do was talk about Ronald; I had just had it, and so I told him off.   ''I asked him, 'How would you like it if everywhere you went, hotels, restaurants, bars, the men's room, people run up to you and shake your hand and tell you how good your brother is, and what he ought to do as President? What the hell kind of life would you have?'    ''I told him I was tired of it and that I was not going to put up with any more and that I was going to start right there; I told him I'd planned to have two drinks, but because of him, I was leaving after one.''

headline: TORONTO REJECTS STUDY OF RAIDS ON HOMOSEXUAL BATHS
abstract: This city's Board of Police Commissioners has decided not to investigate police raids on four homosexual bathhouses that led to a downtown demonstration.   The board's vote, like the police raid last week in which more than 200 people were arrested, increased resentments between Toronto's homosexual population and the city's police force, which has often been accused of poor relations with Toronto's many minority groups.  So far, no one has been seriously injured, but there are increasing concerns that the open hostility on both sides will lead to more violent confrontations in this city of three million.

headline: POTENTIAL BOOK PROJECT OF ABSCAM PROSECUTOR IS ASSAILED BY DEFENSE
abstract: A Justice Department official who supervised the Abscam investigation and prosecuted four current or former members of Congress on resulting corruption charges said yesterday that he might accept an offer to collaborate on a book about the investigation.   An attorney for former Representative John M. Murphy of Staten Island, one of the convicted men, charged that the book possibility had given the prosecutor, Thomas P. Puccio, a ''strong financial interest'' and ''motive'' to ''cover up'' misconduct in the investigation that he said violated the constitutional rights of the convicted men.   The four men and three others convicted with one of them had argued in a three-week hearing that ended Monday in Federal District Court in Brooklyn that the investigation had been so rife with misconduct, including entrapment, that the indictments and convictions should be overturned.

headline: by Robert Pear
abstract: Two law professors told Congress today that Justice Department guidelines governing the use of undercover investigative techniques did not adequately protect privacy or prevent the entrapment of innocent people.   In testimony before the House Judiciary Subcommittee on Civil and Constitutional Rights, Geoffrey R. Stone of the University of Chicago Law School and Louis Seidman of the Georgetown University Law Center said that the guidelines were a commendable first step but did not go far enough.

headline: Theater in Review; 'BOYS IN THE BAND' HITS UNHAPPY CHORD
abstract: FARMINGDALE ''THE Boys in the Band'' is suffering from a sad case of the wrinkles - that malady most dreaded by its mirror-addicted, skin-deep characters.   Mart Crowley's play about a homosexual's birthday party, circa 1968 -then prototypical, now stereotypical -still stings with barbed putdowns, but how is one to put up with all that maudlin selfindulgence? (''I adore cheap sentiment,'' says Michael, the party giver, and you better believe him.)   In point of view (summed up by the near-curtain line: ''You show me a happy homosexual and I'll show you a gay corpse''), the play is as psychologically passe as it is dramatically dated.

headline: Family
abstract: There are 11 different definitions of the word ''family'' in Webster II, but the one closest to its root, familia, which means household, is the second: ''the body of persons who live in one house....''   By that definition a homosexual couple who had lived together in New York City for five years were a family. Wanting the legal and economic advantages belonging to those families that are otherwise defined, they became this month, through adoption, father and son.  The father is four years younger than his new son, which is unusual, if not wholly unique. A father is, in the ninth definition, ''a parent by ties of marriage or adoption.''

headline: The 'Or Else' For Poland Is Made Clearer
abstract: Soviet leaders kept the Poles after school at the party congress last week, and not just to write ''I will not deviate from the socialist line.'' Polish leaders were obliged to agree with Leonid I. Brezhnev, Defense Minister Dimitri F. Ustinov, secret police chief Yuri V. Andropov and other Kremlin heavyweights, on the need for ''urgent'' action to combat threats to Polish socialism and the ''right'' of other Soviet-bloc countries to intervene.   Acting swiftly to forestall another application of the so-called Brezhnev doctrine, used by the Russians to justify their invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968, Polish authorities accused four members of a tiny anti-Communist group of attempting to overthrow the state. They also briefly detained Jacek Kuron, leader of a moderate and more prominent dissident group, KOR, and attempted to serve a summons on another leader, Adam Michnik.

headline: HINSON, FACING A MORALS CHARGE, SHUNS CLAMOR TO QUIT CONGRESS
abstract: Republican and Democratic Party officials in Mississippi continue to call for the resignation of United States Representative John Hinson, arrested last month in Washington on a sodomy charge. But the Fourth District Congressman will hear nothing of it.   The 38-year-old conservative Republican has been in seclusion at Sibley Hospital, a private hospital in Washington where he has been undergoing psychiatric treatment since he pleaded not guilty to attempted sodomy. He has seen only his wife, his attorney, his minister and an administrative assistant, Marshall Hanbury.

headline: American Embassy Says Soviet Set Up 2 Attaches
abstract: The American Embassy, breaking its silence on a two-month-old incident, accused the Soviet authorities today of having subjected two of its military attaches to a ''crude attempt at blackmail and recruitment.''   The embassy commented on reports that Lieut. Col. Thomas A. Spencer and Maj. James R. Holbrook were the targets of an entrapment operation while in the Ukraine in January.

headline: Hinson to Quit Congress, He Tells Governor
abstract: Representative Jon Hinson, Republican of Mississippi, who faces charges of attempted sodomy, announced today that he would resign from Congress April 13.   Mr. Hinson, 38 years old, disclosed the date in a letter to Gov.  William Winter.

headline: Hinson Resigns From House
abstract: Representative Jon Hinson, Republican of Mississippi, who is facing a morals charge, submitted his resignation from Congress today, effective April 13.

headline: HOMOSEXUAL RIGHTS BILL REVIVED; CITY COUNCIL BACKERS PESSIMISTIC
abstract:
City Council President Carol Bellamy and 12 City Council members announced yesterday that they were sponsoring new legislation to ban discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

The legislation was last introduced in the Council in 1978, when it was defeated in committee by a 6-to-3 vote.  The bill is expected to be referred again to the General Welfare Committee, and even its sponsors say it is unlikely to be voted out of committee. The bill was first introduced in 1970, but the only time it was voted on by the full Council was in 1974, when it was defeated 22 to 19.

headline: Bauman Charges Are Dismissed
abstract: The Government has formally dropped charges against Robert E. Bauman, a former Republican Congressman from Maryland who was accused of soliciting sex from a 16-year-old boy. Justice Department officials said Mr. Bauman had avoided prosecution by agreeing to undergo six months of counseling and publicly stating that he was an alcoholic and had ''homosexual tendencies.''

headline: SEXUAL ABUSE OF CHILDREN: A PROBLEM NOT TO BE IGNORED
abstract:
THE experience of childhood sexual abuse is probably the secret most often kept by an adult woman from her family, her friends and even her doctor, therapist or minister. Despite the ease with which we are beginning to talk pubicly about domestic violence, abortion, rape, homosexuality and other previously taboo subjects, incest remains shrouded in silence. Little research has been conducted about incest, and even less has been written about it.

The taboo against incest has been more effective in preventing disclosure than in preventing the act itself. One girl out of every four in the United States will be sexually abused in some way before she reaches 18. A 1967 study by the Children's Division of the American Humane Association estimated that at least 80,000 to 100,000 children are sexually molested each year. In the majority of these cases, the offender was well known to the child, and in about 25 percent of them, the aggressor was a relative.

These estimates were based on New York City police records and the experience of social workers in a child-protection agency. They are, therefore, projections based on observing poor and disorganized families who lack the resources to preserve secrecy. There is reason to believe, however, that most incest in fact occurs in intact nuclear families and never comes to the attention of social agencies.

headline: Mormon Church Elder Calls Homosexuality an Addiction
abstract: Homosexuality is ''an acquired addiction,'' like drugs and alcohol, and would not be so pervasive if children had happy home lives, a Mormon official said today.   Elder Hartman Rector Jr. of the church's First Quorum of the Seventy told thousands gathered for the closing session of the faith's 151st Annual General Conference that he did not believe ''promoters of homosexuality'' who said they were born that way.

headline: REFUSING TO JAIL A WHITE IS CALLED RACIST BY KOCH
abstract: A decision by a Criminal Court judge that a 23-year-old white man should not go to jail ''because the State of New York could not guarantee his safety in prison surroundings'' was criticized yesterday by Mayor Koch and other officials as racist.   The judge, Stanley Gartenstein, had ruled that the man - David Ross, who had been convicted of harassment and resisting arrest - would not be sentenced to jail on Rikers Island even though he had ''richly earned a sentence of incarceration.''   He said in a four-page opinion that Mr. Ross ''would be immediately subject to homosexual rape and sodomy and to brutalities from fellow prisoners such as make the imagination recoil in horror.''   He continued: ''In short, while incarceration is merited, rape, torture and brutality are not. We take judicial notice of defendant's slight build, his mannerisms, dress, color and ethnic background and are cognizant of the unfortunate realities that he would not last for 10 minutes at Rikers Island.''

headline:
NEW JERSEY OPINION;
THE AVERAGE CRIMINAL IS AN AMATEUR
abstract:
IN MARCH 1974, tens of thousands of American youths playfully removed their clothes and ran, jogged, pranced and bicycled through streets, libraries, schools and other public places.

Indecent exposure is a crime. Some arrests were made, and some cases went to court.  On the whole, however, ''streakers'' were not considered sex offenders by the general public. And they did not think of themselves that way; for them, streaking was a lark.

headline: Court Rules Homosexual Can Be Granted Citizenship
abstract: A native of West Germany who is a homosexual cannot be denied United States citizenship because of his sexual preference, a Federal appeals court ruled today.   The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit said that Federal District Judge Oren R. Lewis erred in refusing to give citizenship rights to Horst Nemetz, who now operates a hairstyling salon in Springfield, Va.

headline: Around the Nation; Mrs. King to Seek Eviction Of Woman in Sex Dispute
abstract: An attorney for Billie Jean King says a suit will be filed soon against a woman who has sued the tennis star with the allegation that the two lived together in a homosexual relationship in the early 1970's.   The attorney, Dennis Wasser, said that Mrs. King's suit would seek to have Miss Barnett evicted from a house owned by Mrs. King and her husband, Larry.

headline: WILLIAMS'S TRIAL IS THE LAST OF 8 MAJOR ABSCAM CASES
abstract: Abscam was the most sweeping undercover investigation of political corruption ever undertaken by the Justice Department - a two-year, multimillion-dollar inquiry that involved scores of agents, secret meetings, phony sheiks, hidden cameras, bribes and a parade of Congressmen.   It sprawled over cities in four states, unfolding in hotel rooms, airport lounges, private houses and even aboard a yacht. It generated dramatic confrontations and scenes of comic relief. And it raised many legal and ethical questions - some still not resolved - over possible entrapment, self-incrimination and anonymous leaks to the press.

headline: THE LESBIAN MOTHER: NEW FRANKNESS
abstract:
LESBIAN motherhood is becoming a more open life style on the Island, and lesbians who are having difficulty raising their children in two-woman parental relationships or as single parents are seeking counseling from social agencies and private psychotherapists in increasing numbers.

''Since the American Psychiatric Association has recently recognized that homosexuality is not a pathology, people have become more comfortable in acknowledging their homosexuality, and have felt freer to come to family agencies for help,'' said Jesse Nemtzow, executive director of the Suffolk County Family Service League.

Since many homosexuals still prefer to retain their privacy, the exact number of lesbians on the Island is not known. However, most women's support groups, including Health House in St. James, the Brookhaven Women's Center in Port Jefferson, women's groups at some of the Island's colleges and some local chapters of the National Organization for Women offer lesbian support groups.

A New York State conference for lesbians, sponsored by a collective of lesbians on the Island called Lavender Visions, was held recently at the Empire State College campus in Old Westbury.

headline: Trial of Ex-Rep. Hinson Put Off
abstract: The trial of former Representative Jon C. Hinson, Republican of Mississippi, who is charged with attempted sodomy, was rescheduled today for June 1.

headline: Turkey Begins Campaign Against Homosexuality
abstract: Turkey's security forces, which have been waging a resolute campaign against terrorism, separatism and anarchy, have now struck out against male homosexuals.   The Istanbul police raided the downtown Beyoglu district last weekend, closing down 11 places of entertainment that were said to illegally employ male homosexuals.   At the same time, 22 male homosexuals were taken into custody, detained for 24 hours and removed from the Istanbul area amid scenes of protest and confusion.

headline: DECEPTION DENIED BY REPORTER FOR VOICE
abstract: Teresa Carpenter, a reporter for The Village Voice, says there was no attempt to deceive readers in one of her stories that last month won the Pulitzer Prize for feature writing.   One passage in the article, which was about the murder of former Representative Allard K. Lowenstein by a one-time protege, Dennis Sweeney, implied that Miss Carpenter had interviewed Mr. Sweeney when in fact she had not, according to James A. Wechsler, a columnist for The New York Post, and Mr. Lowenstein's brother, Larry.   Mr. Lowenstein, a Democrat, was a United States Representative from Long Island, serving from 1969 through 1971.  In an interview Saturday night, Miss Carpenter defended the passage, which dealt with allegations that Mr. Lowenstein years before had made an unsuccessful homosexual advance to Mr. Sweeney, and with speculation about the influence of the incident in the murder and on Mr. Sweeney, who was judged insane after the slaying.
