headline: HOUSE PANEL REBUFFS REAGAN AND BACKS KEEPING LEGAL AID FOR POOR
abstract: The House Judiciary Committee, by a 22-to-6 vote today, rejected the Reagan Administration's plan to eliminate Federal financing of legal aid for poor people.   The bill approved by the committee, however, would reduce financing for the independent Legal Services Corporation to $260 million for each of the next two years, from the current $321 million, and would place new restrictions on federally financed legal aid lawyers.   The restrictions prohibit strikes by legal aid lawyers, call for greater control over local programs by the corporation's board, which is appointed by the President, and by state and local bar associations, and would limit class-action suits and lobbying.   The committee bill would also bar legal aid lawyers from litigating on behalf of women seeking abortions, unless the women's lives were threatened, and from litigating for known illegal aliens and persons seeking to legalize homosexuality.

headline: WILLIAMS INQUIRY COUNSEL NAMED
abstract: The Senate Select Committee on Ethics named Robert S. Bennett, a Democrat, today as special counsel for its investigation of Senator Harrison A. Williams Jr.   The chairman of the ethics panel, Senator Malcolm Wallop, Republican of Wyoming, announced the selection of Mr. Bennett, a local lawyer.   Senator Wallop said at a news conerence that the committee's investigation would not become enmeshed in the larger legal issues of due process and entrapment.

headline: 2D DEVICE IS FOUND
abstract: A 20-year-old man was fatally injured yesterday morning when a bomb exploded in a men's room at the Pan American World Airways Terminal at Kennedy International Airport minutes after a warning had been telephoned by a man who said he represented a Puerto Rican independence group.   Hours later, another ''explosive device,'' apparently placed after a search had been made, was found near Gate 18 at the same terminal, delaying evening flights and causing an evacuation for nearly three hours.   The Terrorist Task Force, a joint investigative unit of the New York police and the Federal Bureau of Investigation, reported that a group calling itself the Puerto Rican Armed Resistance had taken responsibility for the explosion.   The group was the same one that said it was responsible for setting off two pipe bombs in a public locker room at Pennsylvania Station on Dec. 21, a task force official said . No separate call was received prior to the discovery of the second explosive device shortly after 6 P.M.

headline: WHEN A CELEBRITY BECOMES NOTORIOUS
abstract: Flip Wilson. Roberto Duran. Marilyn Chambers. Anita Bryant. And now Billie Jean King. All these celebrities have found themselves thrust into controversy that subsequently earned them a frown of disapproval from the marketing world in which they had become involved.   Advertisers set great store by pitchmen who are recognizable, credible and squeaky clean - all the better to move that soda pop, cold cream and starch. When a celebrity's life becomes blemished, marketers are not slow to disassociate themselves.   ''The ad business is the straightest business there is,'' remarks Lloyd Kolmer, who lines up celebrities for ad agencies. ''It doesn't want any shock waves going through it that would hurt a client's image. The company image is the key.''

headline: ABSCAM AS AN UPDATED VERSION OF 'PARADISE
abstract: LOST' To the Editor:     The concern about possible ''entrapment'' of Abscam convicts expressed in your May 5 editorial reminds me of a similarly fretful question raised in Milton's ''Paradise Lost.''   v.   hy does God allow Satan to slip through ''the facile gates of hell too slightly barred'' and permit him to tempt Adam and Eve?  Milton's answer was plain and relevant.

headline: Teen-Agers Accused In Hempstead Rape
abstract: Two Hempstead teen-agers were arrested and charged with the rape, sodomy and robbery of a 28-year-old woman here, according to the Nassau County police.

headline: Around The Nation; Hinson Pleads No Contest To Oral Sodomy Charge
abstract: Former Representative Jon C. Hinson of Mississippi today pleaded no contest in District of Columbia Superior Court to a charge of attempted oral sodomy involving a Library of Congress employee in a House office building restroom last February.   Accompanied by his attorney, Mr. Hinson appeared briefly before Judge David L. Norman.

headline: Notes on People; Anita Bryant May Move
abstract: When last heard from in September, Anita Bryant, having ended her marriage of 20 years, had left Miami and returned to her native Oklahoma.

headline: 10,000 in Boston March For Homosexual Rights
abstract: More than 10,000 supporters of rights for homosexuals marched through Beacon Hill and rallied on The Common today in the annual Gay and Lesbian Pride parade.   The participants, some in costumes, carried banners, sang, clapped and danced their way through the city under a gray sky to show solidarity and protest elimination by Mayor Kevin H. White of a city office charged with liaison with Boston's homosexual community.   The authorities had sought to divert the route from Beacon Hill and downtown areas, saying that it would disrupt business and traffic, but the parade's organizers obtained an injunction against the change.

headline: The Region; Prosecutor Quizzed In Abscam Hearing
abstract: A lawyer for Senator Harrison J. Williams of New Jersey sought to pinpoint when the Federal Government decided to seek an indictment against his client in the Abscam investigation.   The lawyer, George Koelzer, questioned a special Federal prosecutor about the timing of the indictment during a hearing in Federal District Court on allegations that Senator Williams and a codefendant, Alexander Feinberg, a Cherry Hill, N.J., lawyer, were victims of illegal entrapment and Government misconduct. Both men were convicted of bribery and conspiracy in the Abscam case on May 1.

headline: The Region; Del Tufo Tells Court Of Abscam Concern
abstract: Robert J. Del Tufo, who was United States Attorney for New Jersey at the time of the Abscam investigation, testified that he was ''deeply concerned about some of the investigative techniques'' used against Senator Harrison A. Williams Jr. of New Jersey in the undercover Federal inquiry.   The former prosecutor testified in Federal District Court at a hearing in which the Senator, who was convicted on nine counts of bribery and conspiracy, is contending he was a victim of illegal entrapment in the case.

headline: Around the Nation; Judge Rules Against Barring Homosexuals From U.S.
abstract: A Federal district judge ruled today that the Government could not exclude people from entering the United States just because they were homosexuals.   In granting a preliminary injunction, Judge Robert Aguilar said that the constitutional rights of the plaintiffs, Lesbian-Gay Freedom Day Committee Inc. and others, had been threatened by an Immigration and Naturalization Service policy of blocking homosexuals or those accused of being homosexual from visiting the country.   The judge said that the injunction would result in ''no threat to the national security or law enforcement.''

headline: Around the Nation; Oregon Jury Convicts Man Of Murder and Sodomy
abstract: A 30-year-old former college football star was convicted today on one count each of murder and attempted murder and two counts of sodomy.   Randall B. Woodfield of Springfield, Ore., was convicted in the fatal shooting of Shari Hull, 20, and the wounding of Lisa Garcia, 21, while the two women were cleaning an insurance office in the Salem area last Jan. 18.

headline: BELEAGURED TEACHER MAY GET JOB BACK
abstract: LAST October, following a decision by Dr. Fred G. Burke, the state's Commissioner of Education, John Gish lost what might be his last chance to become a teacher again. After seven years as an English teacher at Paramus High School and eight as an administrator there, he found himself standing on an unemployment line.   Mr. Gish, who has publicly advocated the cause of homosexual rights, says that he lost the two jobs because of his superiors' irrational fears about homosexuals.   The Paramus Board of Education, which had pressed for Mr. Gish's expulsion, said that his stature as a political activist for ''gay liberation'' was likely to cause confusion and anxiety among his students, especially those with sexual identity problems. Citing evidence from a psychiatrist who found Mr. Gish to suffer from ''angry paranoid thinking,'' the board declared him unfit to teach.

headline: HOMESEXUALS PARADE UP FIFTH AVE. IN CELEBRATION
abstract: Twelve years ago yesterday Morty Manford was 18 years old and a patron in the Stonewall Inn, a homosexual bar in Greenwich Village, when the police raided it in the early morning, setting off a riot by 300 young men in which 13 were arrested and four police officers injured. It marked the beginning of the homosexual rights movement.   Yesterday, Mr. Manford, a third-year student at the Benjamin N.  Cardozo School of Law at Yeshiva University, walked shirtless up the middle of Fifth Avenue with his mother, Jeanne, and tens of thousands of other homosexual men and women, some of their parents and some of their friends.

headline: CONGRESS PUNISHES HOMOSEXUAL CITIZENS
abstract: To the Editor:     The action of Congress to bar one specific group of tax-paying Americans from free legal services is unconscionable. We refer to the House's 281-124 vote on June 18 to bar the Legal Services Corporation from pressing cases in which homosexuality is an issue.

headline: RARE CANCER SEEN IN 41 HOMOSEXUALS
abstract: Doctors in New York and California have diagnosed among homosexual men 41 cases of a rare and often rapidly fatal form of cancer. Eight of the victims died less than 24 months after the diagnosis was made.    The cause of the outbreak is unknown, and there is as yet no evidence of contagion. But the doctors who have made the diagnoses, mostly in New York City and the San Francisco Bay area, are alerting other physicians who treat large numbers of homosexual men to the problem in an effort to help identify more cases and to reduce the delay in offering chemotherapy treatment.

headline: Ideas & Trends in Summary; RARE CANCER IN HOMOSEXUALS
abstract: A series of statistics issued by the Federal Centers for Disease Control in Atlanta last week brought fear to homosexual men and a challenge to epidemiologists and cancer researchers. Doctors in New York and California have diagnosed 41 cases, going back 30 months, of a rare and often rapidly fatal cancer, Kaposi's Sarcoma, which can appear as violet-colored spots on the skin, infect the lymph glands and then spread throughout the body.

headline: MISSISSIPPI TO CHOOSE SUCCESSOR TO HINSON TODAY
abstract: With both sides happy to make President Reagan's budget the issue, tomorrow's special Congressional election in Mississippi's Fourth District approximates a referendum on those policies on territory friendly to the President and his party.   Republicans have held this seat since 1972, and Liles B. Williams, their candidate to replace Jon C. Hinson, who resigned April 15 after being arrested for attempted sodomy, is better known and better financed than the Democrat, Mayor Wayne Dowdy of McComb.   Mr. Dowdy made it into tomorrow's runoff with only 25 percent of the vote in the nonpartisan primary June 23, to 45 percent for Mr.  Williams. To score an upset, Mr. Dowdy will have to manage the difficult feat of pulling a large black vote without alienating rural whites, a task that has made the Voting Rights Act a significant but intricate issue for him.

headline: Around the Nation; Homosexual Loses Bid To Become Scout Leader
abstract: A Superior Court judge today turned down a 19-year-old homosexual's request that the Boy Scouts of America be ordered to accept him as an adult troop leader.   Judge Robert Weil ruled that the Boy Scouts was a voluntary, private organization that did not have to allow Timothy Curran of Oakland to become a troop leader.

headline: About New York officer; ON BEACH PATROL, HEAT'S THE LEAST OF THE PROBLEMS
abstract: The mass baptisms are no problem; neither is nudism, which has been abandoned in favor of the impossibly tiny swimsuits of the day.  There are occasional drunken brawls, a spate or two of what is classified as ''public lewdness'' and some hubcap thefts. People park willy-nilly, and lost children, their hair wet with salt water and tears, wander in off the boardwalk. A dismembered body was found in a trash bag last month, but it was not considered a major problem.   ''There's our main problem,'' said Capt. Peter Pieroni, pointing at four cases of warm beer, wrapped and tagged, on a table in the back of his station house.

headline: JACK LEMMON: BEHIND THE SMILE
abstract: John Culhane, a writer and film historian, is the author of a book on movie special effects to be published by Ballantine this fall. By John Culhane ack Lemmon, in his temporary dressing room in a gas station in Agoura, Calif., demonstrated how he would deliver his first speech to Walter Matthau in the film ''Buddy Buddy'' - if he could get away with it.   ''Matthau is a hit man who pulls into the gas station to use the men's room,'' said Lemmon. ''But I'm already there, on my way to try to reconcile with my wife, who has abandoned me for the head of a sex clinic. Matthau rattles the knob, he knocks. Finally, I come out and say, 'Sorry - I was throwing up. I have this nervous stomach.' ''   For a brief moment, Lemmon seemed about to encore his act. '' 'Tried everything. They say it's psychosomatic - because of my wife.' ''

headline: JUDAIC CONVERSINS AND LAW OF RETURN
abstract: To the Editor:    Agudath Israel's stand on amending the Law of Return in Israel (news story July 10, ''U.S. Jews Worry About Begin's Allies) has been a focal point of controversy and considerable misunderstanding. Since millions of Jews as well as the general public are concerned about this policy, it is important that clarity prevail.   he Law of Return, as it stands, grants immediate citizenship and other privileges to any Jew from anywhere in the world who elects to settle in Israel. This applies equally to Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and secular Jews alike. A Jew is a Jew, and the fact that he may deviate from classical halachic practice or doctrine does not diminish his or her standing as a Jew. No one seeks to restrict the rights of non-Orthodox Jews as individuals.

headline: The Region; 2 Men Held in L.I.  On Sex Charges
abstract: A rented house in Baldwin Harbor was used as a haven where young boys were taken and sexually abused, officials said. Two men were arrested there Saturday night and detectives seized a large number of videotapes made there that showed men engaged in sexual acts with boys 8 to 15 years old.   Arrested at the house was the tenant, Martin Swithinbank, 53, and Jerry Fox, 32, of Kingston, Pa. Mr. Swithinbank was charged with sodomy, and Mr. Fox was accused of sexual abuse.

headline: EXCERPTS FROM RULING BY FEDERAL JUDGE UPHOLDING THE ABSCAM CONVICTIONS
abstract: Following are excerpts from the ruling by District Judge George C.  Pratt in which he upheld the convictions of seven Abscam defendants: Entrapment as a Matter of Law   All defendants urge, as a primary contention, that the indictment should be dismissed because the Abscam investigation did not uncover criminal conduct, but instead created and instigated it. This argument challenges the essential nature of the Government's ''sting'' operation, which presented to defendants a false and fictitious but convincing ''scenario'' of a wealthy sheik willing to pay cash for promises of assistance in his immigration to the United States. Defendants argue that this scenario induced them to participate in criminal events they otherwise would not have engaged in, simply because absent the Government's actions they would not have had the opportunity to do so - at least with this sheik.

headline: CHURCH FOR HOMOSEXUALS ASKS TO JOIN COUNCIL
abstract: A church organized 13 years ago to accept practicing homosexuals has grown to more than 170 congregations in the United States and overseas, and is now applying for membership in the National Council of Churches.   The Rev. Karen Ziegler, pastor of the 90-member Manhattan congregation of the group, the Metropolitan Community Church, says many churches in her denomination feel isolated from the mainstream of Christianity and want to establish contacts with other believers.   The church began in 1968 when the Rev. Troy Perry, a Pentecostal minister, formed a congregation for Christians who were openly homosexual or supported homosexuality. Mr. Perry is now moderator of the board of elders of the Universal Fellowship of Metropolitan Community Churches, which claims about 26,000 members and has headquarters in Los Angeles.   Several hundred delegates and about 500 visitors are expected at the denomination's general conference in Houston from Aug. 3-9.

headline: Insurance Bribery Case Almost Ready for Jury
abstract: Defense lawyers accused the Government of entrapment and depicted Joseph Hauser, an informer, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation as the real villains in summations today in a trial for bribery and conspiracy involving a fund for insurance company workers.   The defense is to resume its closing arguments in Federal District Court here tomorrow.

headline: GIRL, 12, MISSING FIVE MONTHS, TELLS OF CAPTIVITY IN COAST PIT
abstract: Twelve-year-old Jeana Rodriguez, who was last seen five months ago, returned home yesterday and said she had been held captive by a man who sometimes kept her in a pit, officials said.   The police said today that Miss Rodriguez was uncommunicative at first but later said she had tricked her captor into freeing her.  George J. Dailey, a 36-year-old city maintenance worker, was booked for investigation of kidnapping, sodomy and child molestation, the authorities said.

headline: Around the Nation; Convictions Upheld In Eagleton Extortion
abstract: A Federal appeals court today affirmed the convictions of a niece of Senator Thomas F. Eagleton, Democrat of Missouri, and her attorney on charges of attempting to extort more than $200,000 from the Senator.   Elizabeth Eagleton Weigand and Stephen Poludniak had been found guilty of threatening to start a rumor that the Senator was a homosexual unless he agreed to pay $220,000 for the woman's interest in a business owned by the Eagleton family.

headline: CHURCH COUNCIL LIKELY TO REJECT AN APPLICANT
abstract: Top staff members at the National Council of Churches, the nation's largest ecumenical organization, say they expect the council to reject a membership application by the Universal Fellowship of Metropolitan Community Churches, a denomination that endorses homosexuality.   ''Considering the historical position and doctrinal practices of the communions that compose the National Council of Churches of Christ,'' said the Rev. Arleon Kelley, assistant general secretary of the council, ''it appears to me extremely doubtful that 21 of the necessary members would vote for the inclusion'' of Metropolitan Community Churches.   The denomination decided to apply for membership earlier this year and reaffirmed that decision during a conference in Houston this week. A spokesman for the denomination said a formal application for membership would be made within the next two months.

headline: KINSEY STUDY FINDS HOMOSEXUALS SHOW EARLY PREDISPOSITION
abstract: A major new study of homosexual men and women by the Kinsey Institute for Sex Research has found little or no support for most of the traditional theories about the origins of homosexuality.   In particular, the study of nearly 1,500 people indicates that the parents' role in a child's sexual orientation has been ''grossly exaggerated,'' as have theories that homosexuality results from a lack of heterosexual opportunities or from traumatic heterosexual experiences.   Rather, the researchers conclude that a homosexual orientation usually seems to emerge from a fundamental predisposition, possibly biological in origin, that first appears as a failure to conform to society's stereotype of what it means to be a boy or a girl. Research Method an Issue   The report, to be published as a book, is likely to arouse controversy not only because of its findings, which the authors expect to anger both the psychoanalytic and the homosexual communities, but also because it relies on the memories of those interviewed and on a statistical technique called path analysis that is subject to misuse and can only explore existing notions, not create new ones.

headline: 2 FATAL DISEASES FOCUS OF INQUIRY
abstract: Two rare diseases have struck more than 100 homosexual men in the United States in recent months, killing almost half of them, and a medical study group has been formed to find out why, the national Centers for Disease Control said today.   The disease control agency reported in June and July that 26 cases of Kaposi's sarcoma, a rare form of skin cancer, and 15 cases of pneumocystis, a form of pneumonia caused by a parasitic organism, had been found in homosexual men since January 1980.   Since the midyear reports, new reports have brought the totals to 53 cases of pneumocystis, 47 of Kaposi's sarcoma, and 7 cases in which patients had both diseases. One additional case was that of a woman who contracted pneumocystis. Of the patients whose sexual preference was known, 94 percent were homosexual men.

headline: CORRECTION
abstract: Because of an outdated announce- ment from the Stonewall Repertory Company, an article last Sunday in- correctly reported the casting for the company's first production of the sea- son, ''Risin' to the Love We Need.'' Andre De Shields will not be in it.

headline: Observer; NOW IT CAN BE TOLD
abstract: In the literary world it is open season on the Hollywood dead, and at last I am able to speak.  Until now I have thought it indelicate to disclose that I am Mae West's twin sons. Recently literary allegations that Joan Crawford was a rotten mother and Errol Flynn a homosexual Nazi agent, however, encourage me to believe that the American public is hungering for thenasty facts behind the glamorous myths. My la wyer, moreover, assures me there is no way Mae West can sue from the grave.   The truth is that the Mae West the world knew as eternal bachelorette and sex goddess was, in fact, a mother with double vision. Vanity prevented her from wearing the thick corrective lenses she needed to see the world as it was. As a result she went through life under the impression that I was twins.

headline: COAST KILLINGS TIED TO HOMOSEXUALITY
abstract: William G. Bonin, a 34-year-old truck driver, will go on trial here tomorrow on charges of murdering 12 men and boys in a case that the authorities say throws a spotlight on the little publicized, frequently dangerous world of the male sexual hustler.   This is a city in which the newspapers tend to affix descriptive titles to mass-murder cases. Thus Mr. Bonin is the defendant in the ''Freeway Murders.''

headline: LEONIA PARENTS SUPPORT TEACHER IN MORALS CASE
abstract: LEONIA THE case involving John Anagnosti, who resigned his fourth-grade teaching post at the Anna C. Scott Elementary School here last April over an accusation that he had molested a pupil, is expected to go before a grand jury tomorrow.   Mr. Anagnosti, a 38-year-old bachelor, pleaded guilty to the accusation in March. At the time, he said he was doing so because he wanted to spare the child the emotional trauma of appearing before a grand jury or in a court trial.   In June, however, after receiving help from a group of Leonia parents who raised $7,500 for his defense, Mr. Anagnosti and his lawyer successfully moved in Superior Court in Hackensack to have his plea withdrawn and the case then became one for the grand jury.

headline: DO AS I SAY, NOT AS I DO
abstract: A WOMAN I know is opposed to the Equal Rights Amendment because she is afraid that it will force her to share her bathroom with any unemployed lesbian who voted for Jimmy Carter or Gus Hall.   Other opponents of the amendment are more sophisticated. They oppose those sections of it that would force the drafting of women for combat duty, the hiring of homosexual teachers or the gainful employment of all childless women over the age of 27 1/2.

headline: FLORIDA CURB ON HOMOSEXUALS SURVIVES A TEST
abstract: State Representative Tom Bush was not surprised that a Florida law barring state aid to any university that gives funds, meeting space or recognition to any group advocating ''sexual relations between persons not married to each other'' survived its first judicial test, in a state circuit court last week.    ''It was a very carefully drafted and handled piece of legislation,'' said the 33-year-old Republican legislator from Fort Lauderdale, who sponsored the measure with State Senator Alan Trask of Winterhaven. ''Contrary to what the gays might say, we are not a couple of Bible-thumping idiots who parked our brains outside of the Legislature before enacting this.''   The law drafted by Representative Bush and Senator Trask, a 47-year-old Democrat who says he is a born-again Christian, was passed in May as an amendment to the state budget. It has again divided the state on the issue of civil rights for homosexuals, reminiscent of when Anita Bryant, the singer, led efforts to kill a 1977 Dade County ordinance guaranteeing homosexuals equal rights in jobs, housing and public accommodation.

headline: HOSPITAL GROUP ON WARDS I. SUES TO CLOSE MEN'S SHELTER
abstract: An advocacy group for state mental patients in a hospital on Wards Island sued New York City yesterday, seeking to close a shelter for homeless men there and, in the meantime, to force the men off public buses on the island.   The group, the Board of Visitors for Manhattan C hildren's Psychiatric C enter, says that men from the shelter have been wandering ont o the grounds of the hospital, just a few yards away.   In one case, the group contends, a man broke into one of the children's cottages, but did not harm anyone. And hospital workers have complained of vulgar language and lewd behavior by the men on the buses.

headline: CONSERVATIVE PAPER STIRS DARTMOUTH
abstract: Beginning at Dartmouth College in the north woods of New England, and fed by a small group of foundations in Manhattan and a clutch of conservative writers and political figures, a fresh conservative wind is beginning to blow through the campuses of the Ivy League and beyond.   Here at Dartmouth it has brewed a storm, buffeting a liberalminded administration and minority groups of women, blacks, American Indians and homosexual students. It began just over a year ago, with the first issue of a new and independent student newspaper called The Dartmouth Review. Now, inspired by the Dartmouth tabloid, plans are being laid for new papers this year at Harvard, Princeton, Brown and Yale.   These and other new publications, written and edited by graduate and undergraduate students and financed in part by foundation funds, range from old-line conservative to neo-conservative in outlook and from sniping to scholarly in tone.

headline: The Talk of Berkeley
abstract: It was a scene from an earlier age that would warm the heart of a traditionalist. Two lines of bright-faced freshmen at the University of California waited to be presented to the chancellor, I. Michael Heyman, and Mrs. Heyman. Men wearing suits and ties stood in one, and women wearing party dresses were in the other at the annual reception for new students.   A minor crisis occurred when one student, apparently a homosexual activist, tried to have his male roommate introduced in the line of young women, which included wives of students. His attempt was quickly rebuffed and, and unlike the past, there was no shouting of political slogans as university faculty and staff members in formal dress escorted the new students across the room to meet Chancellor and Mrs. Heyman.

headline: G.O.P. Draws Fire for Polling Delegates to Forum on Aging
abstract: The Democrat who heads the House Select Committee on Aging accused the Republican national chairman today of trying to ''pervert and prostitute'' the forthcoming White House Conference on Aging by surveying the political views of about 900 delegates.

headline: On Language; Homogenized Etymology
abstract: Kimble Mead   ''You are waxing prolix in your middle age!'' observes John Simon, my severe brother in wordwatching, about a tiny, little mistake I made a few weeks ago. (It's about time I waxed prolix; poor Roth has been suffering from waxy buildup.)   In a piece about ''geezer power,'' designed to draw fire from golden oldies, I wrote: ''If lesbians argue that 'homosexual' should be limited to men, I would put up a feeble fight - arguing that the homo is the same as the 'man' in 'mankind' and covers women, too.  ...''   No letters from geezers. But 208 letters, six postcards and a telex from people who know the difference between Latin and Greek derivations.   ''Egad, sir, did you ever take Greek?'' wires Christian P. Hansen, a word-processing supervisor from the Bronx. ''The 'homo' in 'homosexual' comes not from the Latin word meaning 'man,' but from the Greek homos, meaning 'same.' The most that the Latin homo and the English prefix 'homo' have in common is that they are homonyms.''

headline: Suspect in Nun's Rape Is Held Without Bail
abstract: A judge ordered yesterday that one of two men charged with the rape and mutilation of a 31-year-old nun be held without bail and be placed under a suicide watch.   The suspect, Max Lindeman, 23 years old, of 62 East 125th Street, appeared before the judge, Criminal Court Judge Francis X. Egitto, in Manhattan on charges of rape, sodomy, assault, burglary and robbery in the attack.

headline: No Headline
abstract: ACTION ON TAXES AND RIGHTS REJECTED BY NATION'S VOTERS   (By The Associated Press) - Proposed tax breaks for private school pupils in the District of Columbia, a $750 million highway bond in West Virginia, and a homosexual rights measure in Palo Alto, Calif., were among measures that went down to defeat Tuesday in ballot contests around the country.   Meanwhile, two possible Democratic Presidential candidates, Gov.  John D. Rockefeller 4th of West Virginia and Gov. John Y. Brown Jr.  of Kentucky, found themselves on the losing side of ballot propositions in their states.   In West Virginia, a $750 million highway bond strongly backed by Governor Rockefeller was soundly defeated. Voters apparently balked at the spending proposal, favoring the argument that the state could ill afford a new debt.

headline: Art; A SLIM, BUT WELCOME, GROSZ SHOW
abstract: MADISON GEORGE GROSZ was born in Berlin in 1893 and he died there (in the western part) 66 years later. Having left Germany during the 30's as a ''degenerate artist,'' he had returned a few years before his death as a highly respected figure, fit to be elected Extraordinary Member of the Berlin Academy of Art.   The intervening period was spent as a citizen of the United States, where he taught for many years at the Art Students League and where, in 1954, he enjoyed a retrospective at the Whitney Museum.   There have been many posthumous shows of Grosz's work, of which that now (through Nov. 14) at the Korn Gallery of Drew University is the most recent. It's a meager affair, consisting mainly of the lithographed drawings that the artist customarily issued in portfolios and a couple of original works in pencil and they are pinned to the walls unframed and skimpily documented.

headline: The City; The Police Blotter
abstract: A Queens man already in custody on charges of robbery and sodomy was charged with the sexual assault and strangulation of a bank worker last month. The suspect, Chris Aniades, 23 years old, was in the Queens House of Detention when he was charged with abducting Doreen Vitale on Oct. 15 and killing her.

headline: 'MAJORITY' VS. GAYS
abstract: Even a quick look at events in Washington and around the country shows that the Christian right's attack on gay civil rights is taking on new life and intensity. The outcome is uncertain, but two things are clear: The Moral Majority will stop at nothing to make scapegoats of gay people, and the gay community is becoming more united as a result. In this climate, nothing less than extending civil rights laws to cover gays will end the political and moral outrages coming into view.   The clearest signal of the Moral Majority's intentions came Oct. 1 when it persuaded the House of Representatives to overturn a revised sex-assault bill recently passed by the District of Columbia city council that decriminalized sodomy between consenting adults in private. The measure, which had been requested by Congress and was similar to measures already in effect in at least 25 states, drew support from a coalition that included the National Conservative Political Action Committee and Washington's ''Mother of the Year.'' There was no reason to believe that Congress would intervene to block the act during the pro forma 30-day waiting period before it became law.

headline: BILL ON HOMOSEXUAL RIGHTS SPARKS EMOTIONAL DEBATES
abstract: A proposal to ban discrimination against homosexuals turned a City Council committee hearing into a long, loud display of emotions yesterday as supporters and opponents showed up in large numbers.   The list of supporters was led by Mayor Koch, State Attorney General Robert Abrams and City Comptroller Harrison J. Goldin. Most prominent among the opponents were representatives from the Archdiocese of New York and orthodox Jewish groups.

headline: The City; Two Are Indicted In Rape of Nun
abstract: Two Manhattan men were indicted yesterday on charges of raping a 30-year-old nun last month, and District Attorney Robert M.  Morgenthau of Manhattan said he would seek stiff consecutive sentences if the men were convicted.   The accused - Max Lindeman, 23 years old, and Harold Wells, 22 - were accused in a 17-count indictment with rape, sodomy, aggravated sexual abuse, assault, robbery and burglary in the Oct. 10 attack at an East Harlem convent.

headline: Teller Is Dismissed From Job For Opposiing Charity Drive
abstract: A part-time bank teller was dismissed from her job because she refused to make a voluntary donation to United Way, the bank president confirmed Friday.   ''I think I'm right about this, and I'm going to stand by what I think is right,'' said Richard Deckerhoff, president of the First Federal Savings and Loan, Allegany County's largest bank.   Terri Ware said she had refused to donate the money in this year's campaign because she had said that United Way supported organizations that approve of abortions and homosexual rights.

headline: A LOOK AT WHO RUNS THE TRAIN STATIONS
abstract: AS most commuters would assume, Conrail, as contractor for the M.T.A., is responsible for the maintenance of all train-boarding facilities - the stairways and platforms, the track overpasses and tunnels. But Westchester's commuter train stations are the responsibility of their owners - and in many cases the stations themselves are not run by Metropolitan Transportation Authority, but are in the care of villages, private concerns or individuals.   And most commuters, as unhappy as they may become with the track and signal difficulties that cause delays in the train service provided by Conrail - the Consolidated Rail Corporation, the Federal successor to the region's bankrupt private railroads -can attest that some of the non-operating problems facing the contractors are pervasive.   The dignity of aging buildings with wooden benches, for example, has been diminished at many stations by the indignities of graffiti and vandalism; the operator of New Rochelle's station says that keeping glass panes in the front doors has become a lost cause. And at both New Rochelle and White Plains, the men's rooms have been padlocked because of frequent property damage and also indecent conduct.

headline: CITY COUNCIL VS. HOMOSEXUALS' RIGHTS
abstract: To the Editor:     Once again New Yorkers have witnessed the shameful spectacle of elected officials refusing to enact a civil rights bill that would have protected the rights of lesbians and gay men (''A Panel Kills Bill That Aids Homosexuals,'' news article Nov. 24).   hat such a rebuff to the homosexual community of New York could have occurred in this city, with its important gay community, attests to the power of an extreme moralism that flies in the face of reason and equity.

headline: CITY COUNCIL VS. HOMOSEXUALS' RIGHTS
abstract: To the Editor:     In your Nov. 21 news story about the City Council hearing on gay rights, the view of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese was stated clearly as against gay rights legislation. However, no mention was made of the fact that I presented a vigorous statement in favor.

headline: HOMOSEXUALS FOUND PARTICULARLY LIABLE TO COMMON VIRUSES
abstract: Three studies published today described a cluster of cases in which usually harmless viruses and bacteria can produce fatal illnesses, almost exclusively among homosexual men.   Researchers said the immune systems of many of these men appeared to have been weakened for unknown reasons.  Two-thirds of the total of 19 men in the studies died of viruses that most people are exposed to every day without consequence, the reports in The New England Journal of Medicine said.

headline: CITY COUNCIL DEFEATS A MOVE TO RESTORE HOMOSEXUAL BILL
abstract: An attempt to resurrect a proposal to ban discrimination against homosexuals was defeated by the City Council yesterday. The vote was 24 to 18, with one member absent.   The defeat was the 11th suffered by five different versions of the so-called ''gay rights bill'' in 10 years, including one last month.  Although the hourlong debate lacked much of the emotionalism of earlier sessions, primarily because only 60 seats were available for spectators, the action was an unusual attempt by supporters to achieve something of a legislative end-run around opponents.

headline: HAIG LINKS MOVES AGAINST QADDAFI WITH MORAL ANGER
abstract: Secretary of State Alexander M. Haig Jr. said today that, while Western Europe was entitled to its own view of Libya, the United States had decided that it could no longer carry on ''business as usual'' with a regime that practiced terrorism, ''especially when it is targeted on American officials.''   Faced with widespread European skepticism and opposition to the Reagan Administration's decision to ask Americans living in Libya to return home, Mr. Haig seemed to deviate from the official explanation for the American action by attributing it more to moral outrage than to the safety of Americans.   ''Each nation is entitled to draw its own conclusions with respect to Libyan activity,'' he said, ''but for our part we no longer believe that a double standard with respect to international lawlessness and terrorism, especially when it is targeted on Amerian officials, is a contributor to international peace and stability and the rule of law which we all seek to espouse. And therefore we've taken these minor steps.''

headline: SPOKANE RAPE CASE TAKES FAMILY TOLL
abstract: Last summer Ruth Coe described this eastern Washington city as ''a sweet, homey town,'' but that was before her son, Fred, was convicted of multiple charges of rape.   It was also before Mrs. Coe was herself arrested on charges of trying to hire somebody to kill the man who prosecuted her son and the judge who sentenced him as the ''South Hill rapist.''   The ''hit man'' turned out to be a police lieutenant working under cover. Mrs. Coe's husband, Gordon, a man in his 60's whose newspaper career was ended by the circumstances surrounding his son's conviction on July 30, called his wife's arrest a ''clear case of entrapment.''   ''I had a severely disturbed and distraught wife and they could have just informed me that she had gotten this idea and we could have seen that she got help,'' Mr. Coe said after his 61-year-old wife was jailed.

headline: JUSTICE SYSTEM IN STATE FOUND NEARING CHAOS
abstract: A commission appointed by Governor Carey to study crime issued a gloomy report today on the state's criminal-justice system.   It said it was ''choking on numbers,'' used record-keeping methods that amounted to ''chaos'' and was near ''judicial gridlock'' in its treatment of misdemeanors.   In a preliminary report to Mr. Carey, the Advisory Commission on the Administration of Justice found that the crime rate was so high that in New York City certain crimes, such as burglaries involving sums of less than $5,000, were at one time not investigated. This created what the commission called ''de facto decriminalization of certain crimes by ignoring them.'' The practice stopped, the commission said, only after publicity about it ''created a public uproar.''

headline: HOMOSEXUALS LACK NO CIVIL RIGHT
abstract: To the Editor:    On Dec. 8 you printed letters from Ronald Bayer and Bishop Paul Moore adversely criticizing the recent renewed refusal of a committee of the City Council to report out a bill which would have added ''sexual orientation'' (i.e., homosexuality or heterosexuality) to certain attributes, including race, creed, color, national origin and sex, as forbidden bases of discrimination in employment and in the sale or rental of housing in New York City. On Dec. 10 a discharge petition to place the bill before the full council for a vote was defeated, and the bill is dead for the present.   Both letters, and much other argument in support of the bill, make the fundamental mistake of asserting that in the present state of the law, i.e., without the bill, homosexuals have fewer civil rights than do other people. For example, Bishop Moore quotes a diocesan resolution of the Episcopal Church ''support(ing) laws guaranteeing homosexuals all civil rights guaranteed to other citizens.''

headline: Williams Loses Entrapment Plea
abstract: A Federal judge concluded last week that Harrison A. Williams Jr.  is too smart for his own good, thereby increasing the odds that the New Jersey Democrat will become the first member since the Civil War to be expelled from the United States Senate.   Mr. Williams had contended that Federal undercover agents in the Abscam investigation illegally entrapped him into agreeing to use his influence to obtain Government contracts for a titanium mine in which he had a concealed interest.

headline: The Process Due Senator Williams
abstract: The excuse the Senate has used to postpone the day of judgment for Harrison Williams is no longer available. Federal Judge George Pratt has now rejected the Senator's motions to throw out his bribery conviction.   Given the Senator's stalling and previous pleas to await the judicial process, it would not be surprising to hear a new refrain for delay: Let's wait for higher courts. Maybe they can find entrapment and other impropriety in the Abscam investigation.

headline: CATHOLICS GET RECORD NUMBER OF ANNULMENTS
abstract: Divorced Roman Catholics in the United States are receiving annulments in record numbers, the result of streamlined procedures for dissolving a marriage by a church trying to end the estrangement of thousands of members.   No longer is it necessary to prove such charges as homosexuality, insanity, deceit or bigamy for a marriage to be declared null in the eyes of the Catholic Church. An annulment means basically that two people may have attempted to make a marriage, but did not marry in the eyes of the church.   ''Annulments are no longer just for the world of the rich or wellconnected,'' said LaSalle Caron, a Washington real estate man and the father of two, who had his 13-year marriage annulled two years ago.

headline: DEFENSE LAWYER FOR 'GANG OF FOUR' RETAINS HIS FAITH IN CHINA
abstract: Like most of the lawyers in China, Ma Rongjie suffered grievously during the Cultural Revolution, a time when the legal profession was deemed degenerate and parasitic.   He spent 10 months in solitary confinement and seven years of hard labor on a farm - sustained only, he says, by the hope that a new and more moderate China would one day need his services again.   Mr. Ma's faith was borne out, and he is now one of the most prominent lawyers in China. But his vindication came with a twist: In late 1980, he was ordered by Chinese authorities to defend the Gang of Four, the very individuals who had apparently thrown both the country and his own life into turmoil.   It was a case in which not only several people accused of counterrevolutionary activities but also China's new legal system - which bears little resemblance to the Western system of justice - were put on trial.

headline: LOS ANGELES JURY CONVICTS MAN ACCUSED IN 10 KILLINGS
abstract: William Bonin, a 34-year-old truck driver, was convicted today of murdering 10 boys and young men and abandoning their bodies near freeways in Los Angeles County in 1979 and 1980.  He was acquitted of killing two other young men in the heavily publicized freeway killings case that haunted the homosexual community here for months.   The jury in Superior Court that convicted Mr. Bonin also decided that because of the multiple murders, and because several victims had been robbed, the case involved ''special circumstances.'' This meant that he would be sentenced under a California law requiring the use of the death penalty or a life sentence without possibility of parole. The jurors will decide on the penalty after a hearing to begin Thursday.

headline: SUSPECT IS HELD IN SLAYINGS OF 6 IN LAST 6 WEEKS
abstract: A 21-year-old Manhattan man was arrested yesterday and charged early today with committing six murders since Dec. 4. The victims included a performer in a light opera company who was shot to death in Central Park and an investment adviser who was killed in his apartment-office in the financial district.   An Assistant District Attorney, Elliot Jacobson, said that the man, David Bullock, whom he described as a ''homosexual prostitute,'' had admitted to detectives the six murders and four other shootings.   Mr. Jacobson told Judge William Davis of Criminal Court, who presided at the arraignment proceedings held at 12:30 A.M. today, that Mr.  Bullock had murdered without provocation.

headline: AUSTIN VOTING ON WHETHER A LANDLORD CAN REFUSE TO RENT TO HOMOSEXUALS
abstract: To Dr. Steve Hotze, the basic question is strictly one of public morality: Should homosexuals be denied official support so that they will find it more difficult to expand their influence over the young people of the capital of Texas? He and his allies emphatically say yes.   To Dr. Hotze's adversary, Robb Southerland, it is a different question, one of human rights: Should Austin disgrace itself by becoming the first city in the country to legalize discrimination by landlords against tenants who are homosexuals? He and his allies, just as emphatically, say no.   On Saturday, voters will decide whether to amend the city's fair housing ordinance to read, ''It shall not be unlawful to deny housing on the basis of sexual orientation.'' They will do so because a group called Austin Citizens for Decency, led by Dr. Hotze, a 31-year-old general practitioner with six children, obtained 27,000 signatures on petitions Parallels to Florida Vote   It is believed that no city has explicitly made it legal for landlords to deny housing to prospective tenants because of sexual identity. Five years ago voters in Dade County, Florida, rejected an ordinance of opposite intent, one that prohibited discrimination against homosexuals, after a bitter challenge led by Anita Bryant, the singer. But there the next step was not taken.

headline: AUSTIN VOTERS REJECT AMENDMENT ALLOWING HOUSING DISCRIMINATION
abstract: The voters of Austin Saturday overwhelmingly rejected a proposal that would have made the Texas capital the first city in the nation to legalize housing discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.   The proposed amendment to the city's Fair Housing Ordinance was defeated almost 2 to 1 by the voters of this central Texas community, which has a reputation for tolerating diverse life styles.   In an unusually high turnout, 29 percent of this city's 199,390 registered voters participated despite bitterly cold temperatures.  The final tally was 36,239 against the proposal and 20,997 in favor of it.

headline: PSYCHIATRISTS ON HOMOSEXUALITY: VIGOROUS DISCORD VOICED AT MEETING
abstract: NEARLY a decade after American psychiatry deleted homosexuality from its list of mental illnesses, the profession remains polarized in its views, to judge by the vigorous debate at a major symposium on homosexuality last weekend.   Some professionals, primarily classical psychoanalysts, insist that homosexuality is inherently abnormal; others more sociologically oriented maintain it is a normal variant of human sexual behavior.  Some say dissatisfied homosexuals should be offered therapy to help them become heterosexuals; others, especially homosexual psychiatrists, say unhappy homosexuals should be helped only to become happier with their sexual orientation.   Whatever their views, nearly all denounced homophobia (fear and hatred of homosexuality) and prejudice, which they said pervades the psychiatric profession as well as society at large. Dr. Judd Marmor, a Los Angeles psychiatrist who is a professor emeritus at the University of Southern California, asserted that homosexual physicians were still denied res idency training in psychiatry by mosthospitals and that no psychoanalytic institute would knowingly accepta homosexual trainee.

headline: WITNESS IN ATLANTA KILLINGS LINKS DEFENDANT TO VICTIM
abstract: A 15-year-old black youth testified today that Wayne B. Williams fondled him after taking him for a ride in his automobile and that, five months later, he saw Mr. Williams pick up another young black, Lubie Geter, 14, whose partially clad body was found about a month later alongside a county road.   Mr. Williams is not charged in the Geter case, but the teen-ager's testimony today was the first time in the four-week-old trial of Mr.  Williams that the prosecution has hinted at a motive for the two murders with which he is charged. Mr. Williams has denied that he is a homosexual.   Because the youth who testified today was a juvenile, Judge Clarence Cooper of Fulton County Superior Court allowed him to appear as a witness without publicly disclosing his name or address.  However, the judge imposed no restrictions on his picture being taken outside the courtroom by news photographers.

headline: Work-Plan Inmate Flees and Is Seized
abstract: While taking part in a program in which Rikers Island inmates are released for part of the day to clean Parks Department facilities, a prisoner walked into the men's room of a Brooklyn recreational center and ran out a back door. He was recaptured later in the day.

headline: Florida Court Upsets Curb on Campus Life
abstract: The Florida Legislature violated the First Amendment rights of students last year when it threatened to withhold state dollars from universities that recognized or provided meeting space to groups advocating a homosexual way of life or sexual relations between unmarried persons, the Florida Supreme Court ruled today.   In unanimously striking down the law, the state court ruled that ''while a sta te might choose not to establish any state-supported institutions of higher learning, it may not make the privilege of attending contingent upon the surrender of constitutional rights.''

headline: APPELLATE COURT REINSTATES TWO OF ABSCAM CONVICTIONS
abstract: A divided Federal appellate court today reinstated the convictions of a Philadelphia city councilman and a former council president on charges growing out of the Federal bribery investigation known as Abscam. The United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit thus ov erturned the ruling of Judge John P. Fullam of United States Di strict Court, who had reversed a jury's verdict against George X.  Sc hwartz, the former Council president, and Harry P. Jannotti, who re signed as the majority leader of the council during the prosecutionbu t is still a member.   The two were judged guilty Sept. 16, 1980, by a jury that found both had conspired to obstruct interstate commerce, by accepting illegal payments in violation of the Hobbs Act. Mr. Schwartz was also convicted of conspiracy in violation of the Federal anti-racketeering law.   Judge Fullam had thrown out the convictions principally on grounds of entrapment, charging that the Government investigators had gone beyond the bounds of due process.

headline: WITNESSES IN ATLANTA DISPUTE HOMOSEXUALITY ISSUE IN TRIAL
abstract: Two defense witnesses testified at the murder trial of Wayne B. Williams today that Mr. Williams had expressed a dislike for homosexuals. Prosecutors have asserted that Mr. Williams is a homosexual and that his sexual preference played a part in the deaths of the two young black men he is accused of killing.   Mr. Williams has pleaded not guilty in the slayings of Nathaniel Cater, 27 years old, and Jimmy Ray Payne, 21, two of 28 young blacks whose deaths over a 22-month period have been investigated by a special police team.

headline: PRESIDENT DEFENDS HIS NOMINATION OF MINISTER TO CIVIL RIGHTS AGENCY
abstract: President Reagan today defended his choice of the Rev. B. Sam Hart as a nominee to the United States Civil Rights Commission, saying that the radio evangelist ''is not against equal rights'' for women.   ''I am quite confident in his quality and his ability for that job,'' Mr. Reagan said at his afternoon news conference.  Mr. Reagan's intention to nominate Mr. Hart to the position on the rights commission has touched off a barrage of controversy. At a news conference in Washington last week, Mr. Hart expressed his opposition to the proposed Federal equal rights amendment and to busing to achieve racial desegregation. He also said that he did not consider homosexuality a civil rights issue.

headline: U.S. JUDGE ASSAILS SENTENCING OF FELONS TO COMMUNITY JOBS
abstract: A Federal judge has assailed the growing number of programs under which nonviolent and white-collar criminals are sentenced to perform community-service work as an alternative to prison. He said that such sentencing would have the ''effect of sending individuals who may be moral degenerates and perverts into ghetto neighborhoods to work with underprivileged children.''   The judge, Henry Bramwell of Federal District Court in Brooklyn, took the position in a statement he distributed to reporters last week. He called the statement an ''addendum'' to an article criticizing so-called alternative-sentencing approaches that he published last month in a legal journal and that he also distributed.

headline: REP. RICHMOND HELPED FUGITIVE GET JOB ON PAYROLL OF HOUSE DOORKEEPER
abstract: An escaped convict got a clerical job in the House of Representatives last year with the help of Representative Frederick W. Richmond of Brooklyn, according to official records and interviews with law enforcement officials and others.   Mr. Richmond, according to these accounts, also found the man a rented room in Washington and gave him use of his car.  The Congressman, through his spokesman, Michael Kahan, acknowledged that he had recommended the man for a job on the payroll of the House Doorkeeper. But Mr. Richmond would not say whether he knew the man was a fugitive and would not answer other questions, his spokesman said.   The convict was arrested in Manhattan last March on a charge of homosexual prostitution shortly after leaving the job with the House. He was later returned to prison in Massachusetts to continue serving a term for assault with intent to kill. He is now being held at the Southeast Correctional Center in Bridgewater, Mass.

headline: BRIEFING
abstract: A Pronouncement Backfires   P ronouncements of the Moral Majority often draw cautious silence from working politicians who might disagree but don't wish to attract the attention of the effective fundamentalist lobbying organization.  However, a recent pronouncement in the Moral Majority Report, which listed 119 members of Congress by name as having ''voted for sodomy,'' was too much for many of them.   At issue was a home-rule bill in which the local government of the District of Columbia sought permission to decriminalize certain sex acts between consenting adults.   Lawmakers such as Representative Millicent Fenwick, Republican of New Jersey, were angered at such a broadside and joined to compose a complaint to Moral Majority, pointing out that the proposed changes were part of a model code already adopted by numerous cities.

headline: Words Fail Him
abstract: Representative Frederick Richmond of Brooklyn ''will have no comment,'' says his press secretary, Michael Kahan.  Throughout his public career, the 58-year-old Brooklyn Congressman has wooed the press and hunted headlines with near-religious fervor, but now he won't say a word about the shroud of scandal that seems to be wrapping itself ever tighter about him.   Carefully detailed newspaper disclosures - by Ralph Blumenthal in The New York Times and Daniel Lehman in The Brooklyn Paper, a community weekly - have laid out damaging allegations against the millionaire businessman-politician about misuse of his corporate funds for private and political ends; about disguised campaign contributions from people who had received large Government contracts with the Congressman's help; and - in the latest revelation - about helping an escaped career criminal from Massachusetts get a clerical job in the House of Representatives.   That convict, Earl Randolph, was caught in Manhattan last year and returned to the Massachusetts prison system, where he had been serving up to 18 years for assault with intent to murder. His arrest here came about while he was sitting in a car belonging to Mr.  Richmond; he was charged with soliciting an undercover policeman for an act of homosexual prostitution for a fee of $30.

headline: HOMOSEXUAL TAKES LEAVE OF A JOB AND OF AN AGONY
abstract: In more than 15 years on state and Federal payrolls, Dan J. Bradley, the departing president of the Legal Services Corporation, always worried first about keeping his secret.  It survived routine background checks by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the relentless grind of the rumor mills in this city of whispers. And, despite some close calls, the chance discovery that might have sidetracked his public service career never happened.    Now, as Mr. Bradley prepares to leave Washington to begin a new life and career in Miami or San Francisco, he has stunned friends and associates with this disclosure: He is a homosexual.   Last Friday, Mr. Bradley wrote letters to close friends around the country to tell them his ''deep dark secret.'' The first letter was to a former dean of students at Mercer University, the Baptist college in Macon, Ga., where Mr. Bradley studied for the ministry before the church's stand on segregation alienated him.

headline: RESIDENTS DIVIDED ON SEALING CAVE
abstract: LAFAYETTE TOWNSHIP FOR several weeks, the sounds of tree frogs and blue herons have echoed through the marshy woodlands at Crooked Swamp here, luring groups of spring visitors - science students, Scout troops, spelunkers, amateur anthropologists and naturalists - to an unspoiled environment surrounding New Jersey's largest cave.   In the aftermath of the fatal entrapment last weekend of Donald Weltner of Perrineville, in Monmouth County, some local residents have proposed that the 1,250-foot-long cave -Crooked Swamp Cave - be sealed.   However, others viewed the proposal as ''an over-reaction'' and said it would end valuable historical and educational opportunities.  A network of caves sprawls more than 100 acres around the site of the accident.

headline: No More Pretending
abstract: Tired of living in ''sheer, unmitigated fear'' of discovery, Dan J. Bradley astonished associates in Washington last week with the disclosure that he was a homosexual. Mr. Bradley, the departing president of the Legal Services Corporation, announced that he would be leaving for quieter places.

headline: By ALVIN KLEIN
abstract: TO observers of the experimental-theater scene, Charles Ludlam has transformed ridiculousness into art. Among other guises, he has appeared in his own plays as a hairy-chested Camille, a fiendish Bluebeard who invents a third gender and a ventriloquist whose dummy really talks back.   The playwright, actor and director, who was born in Floral Park and moved to Greenlawn when he was 10 years old, has been the artistic director of the aptly named and perhaps self-explanatory Ridiculous Theatrical Company since 1967 - with such actresses as Black-Eyed Susan and Mink Stole among the members of the oldest established repertory company in Greenwich Village.   Now showing is ''Secret Lives of the Sexists,'' Mr. Ludlam's ''new farce of modern life,'' in which he plays a macho masseur who gives ''licensed and unlicensed massages,'' pretending to be a homosexual so that his female clientele won't think he is taking advantage of them - and who winds up attending a women's liberation conference in drag.

headline: Engineer Found Guilty Of Abusing His Children
abstract: An aerospace engineer permitted a Superior Court judge to find him guilty of 18 counts of child molestation and sexual perversion Tuesday on the basis of a preliminary hearing.   The engineer, Ron Rongstad, who lived with his wife, mistress and 15 children in Laguna Hills, agreed to allow Judge Everett Dickey to reach a verdict based on the preliminary hearing if 14 of 32 counts were dropped.

headline: Losing on Exotic Bets
abstract: It's disgraceful that New York State's Racing and Wagering Board is unable to mete out justice to jockeys it clearly believes to have been fixing horse races. Most of them are still riding high. It's equally dismaying that the state, like the crooked gamblers, has become lovingly dependent on fancy betting practices that are easy to pervert.

headline: 'A Little Kind of Low Chuckle'
abstract: Not content with describing ''The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn'' as ''racist trash,'' John Wallace, an administrator at the Mark Twain Intermediate School in Fairfax, Va., added that anyone who taught the book was racist too. Speaking for the school's Human Relations Committee, he asked that it be removed from the curriculum.   Carry Mr. Wallace's condemnation to its logical conclusion and Huck Finn's audience is also racist -but we'll bet they don't know it. Instead they are probably reading the tale of the runaway black slave and the runaway white boy (running away from the drunken degenerate who is his father) because it is exciting and beautiful and funny.

headline: LONG SENTENCES SOUGHT FOR REPEAT OFFENDERS
abstract: Jackson Monroe Martin slumped in his chair and stared at the floor. He could not believe he had just been sentenced to 99 years in jail for indecent exposure.   ''I don't think it's right for me to get that much time for that kind of crime,'' said the 42-year-old Mr. Martin, whose 11 prior convictions for burglary enabled the prosecutor to ask for the long sentence. ''Maybe a fine and 30 days, or even a year in the county jail. But not 99 years!''

headline: by Sally Ogle Davis
abstract: Sally Ogle Davis is a Los Angeles based writer.   The day is almost over and in his CBS Studio Center office-dressing room on the edge of the San Fernando Valley, Ed Asner has spent most of it trying not to talk. For the 52-year-old actor, it's an unnatural act, but silence, or as close to it as he can manage, is the Screen Actors Guild president's new ploy in a philosophical battle with the Charlton Heston faction in the guild, and Asner is going to manage it even it if it kills him.   Having been stung by the reverberations his support of the rebels in El Salvador and his commitment to raise $1 million for medical aid to that country have had on union matters, Asner now intones, most un-Asnerlike: ''We no longer wish to conduct the battle in the trades and the media. The opposition will not stop, but we are not going to respond to their accusations and charges, because they are ceaseless.''

headline: Briefing
abstract: A Vote Is a Vote Is a Vote   A host of national and local political figures turned out the other night for the annual banquet of the Gertrude Stein Democratic Club, an influential local homosexual organization.   Mayor Marion S. Barry Jr. of Washington and his wife stopped by, as did nine of the 13 members of the City Council.

headline: SUPPORT GROUPS: HELP AND DEBATE
abstract:
THE setting is a living room on the North Shore. Or metal chairs in a borrowed church basement. The people involved, drinking coffee and listening to one another, appear to be friends.

But they aren't talking about taxes or their latest vacation.  They're discussing what it's like to find out you're adopted at age 37. Or how it feels to be the parent of a hydrocephalic child. Or a homosexual young adult. Or one who has been snatched away by an angry former mate. They're describing their feelings about being widowed, divorced, anxiety-ridden or terminally ill.

And increasingly they are turning not to professionals for help and solace, but to one another. Professionals, for their part, feel that grass-roots support groups can be beneficial. But they also feel that the groups have definite limitations and, in some instances, can be dangerous.

headline: TAPPING THE HOMOSEXUAL MARKET
abstract: Major film studios made a hedged bet this season that the healthy, wealthy and-or wise homosexual was a marketable commodity. Paramount Pictures's ''Partners,'' which opened this weekend, is a comedy about two New York cops (one's straight, the other isn't) who pretend to be lovers to solve a murder. It follows: 20th-Century Fox's ''Making Love'' (a doctor leaves his wife for another man); Warner Bros.'s ''Personal Best'' (two female Olympic teammates fall in love) and ''Deathtrap'' (Michael Caine and Christopher Reeve play lovers), and M-G-M/ U.A.'s ''Victor, Victoria,'' in which Julie Andrews finishes off her nun and governess image by playing a woman pretending to be a man who is a female impersonator.   The challenge was to sell these films without alienating either the general audience or the homosexual audience. Accordingly, the studios' public profile was low. Executives and film makers even denied that their projects were about homosexuality, insisting, for example, that ''Personal Best'' was a look at competition and friendship, while ''Victor, Victoria'' was alleged simply to be an updated version of an old farce.

headline: LEARNING HOW TO RELAX WITHOUT GUILT
abstract:
WHY do I always feel guilty when I'm not doing anything? I mean, what's the big deal? The cat sits around all day and never lifts a paw, yet I feel like a degenerate when I'm idle. Maybe the cat has a better analyst. Who knows. But me, I'm like a kid caught robbing the cookie jar.

My friend Sheila sits for hours devouring the soaps, while curtains are still packed away from her move six months ago. I get nervous if the 4:30 movie sounds inviting. And what about Ginger who, behind closed doors, daily from 2 to 3, hums her mantra, totally relaxes her body and soul, and emerges as if she's had a 10-hour nap. I tried that once, but found it difficult writing my grocery list in the lotus position. Then there's Pam, who takes one day off every other month, her ''sick and tired time,'' she calls it, just to laze, read Redbook and sip tea. She unplugs the phone, puts on her robe and really gets into relaxing.

headline: Guilty Plea Made In Cocaine Case
abstract: A defendant in a Federal cocaine case who had claimed entrapment by Government agents withdrew an earlier not-guilty plea to three drug counts and pleaded guilty to a single conspiracy charge before Judge Thomas C. Platt of District Court in Brooklyn.   Under the plea agreement, the defendant, 29-year-old Joseph Marino, faces a maximum five-year prison sentence and $25,000 fine instead of 15 years and a fine for each count.

headline: 'HAPPY,' PERHAPS; 'GAY'?-WELL...
abstract:
WHEN I was young, a ''gay'' person was someone who laughed a lot and always seemed to enjoy life, and the Gaiety was a theater that catered to the heterosexual fantasies of immature males.

Before the era of ''gay rights,'' few would admit to any degree of affection for persons of the same sex. In a male-dominated culture, few boys over the age of 16 would admit that they were virgins and few unmarried females that they were not.

headline: NEW HOMOSEXUAL DISORDER WORRIES HEALTH OFFICIALS
abstract: ASERIOUS disorder of the immune system that has been known to doctors for less than a year - a disorder that appears to affect primarily male homosexuals - has now afflicted at least 335 people, of whom it has killed 136, officials of the Centers for Disease Control in Atlanta said yesterday. Federal health officials are concerned that tens of thousands more homosexual men may be silently affected and therefore vulnerable to potentially grave ailments.   Moreover, this immune-system breakdown, which has been implicated in a rare type of cancer, called Kaposi's sarcoma, and seems to invite in its wake a wide variety of serious infections and other disorders, has developed among some heterosexual women and bisexual and heterosexual men.   At a recent Congressional hearing, Dr. Bruce A. Chabner of the National Cancer Institute said that the growing problem was now ''of concern to all Americans.''   The cause of the disorder is unknown. Researchers call it A.I.D., for acquired immunodeficiency disease, or GRID, for gay-related immunodeficiency. It has been reported in 20 states and seven countries. But the overwhelming majority of cases have been in New York City (158), elsewhere in New York State (10), New Jersey (14) and California (71).

headline: Church Council Delays Vote on Homosexuals
abstract: The National Council of Churches voted today to wait a year before deciding whether the nation's only homosexual-oriented denomination should be permitted to join the interfaith agency.

headline: The Nation in Summary; Another Judge Knocks Abscam
abstract: The Government's Abscam investigation - praised by some for ferreting out corrupt politicians, damned by others for unfairly entrapping its victims - took one of its sharpest raps yet last week. Characterizing Abscam as a ''loose cannon rolling around on the deck of the criminal justice system,'' Federal district Judge William B.  Bryant overturned the conviction of former Representative Richard Kelly, a Republican from Florida.   Judge Bryant clearly had his doubts from the start. At one point during Mr. Kelly's trial, which ended on Jan. 26, 1981, with his conviction on bribery, conspiracy and other Federal charges, the judge observed that the Government's conduct had ''an odor to it that is absolutely repulsive.'' Last week, expanding on that initial impression in a 25-page opinion, he said that the F.B.I.'s deployment of free-spending make-believe sheiks and videotaping crews ''so deviates from real-world constraints that it (resulted) in a crime which would never have reached fruition but for the Government's involvement.'' Judge Bryant also granted new trials to two men indicted and convicted with Mr. Kelly and were described as middlemen in the alleged bribery scheme. A Justice Department spokesman said the judge's ruling would probably be appealed.

headline: Around the Nation; Church Panel Rules Out Trial of Methodist Bishop
abstract: A Methodist bishop who assigned a homosexual pastor to a Denver church should not be tried on charges of heresy and disobedience, a church investigative panel decided today.   The seven-member committee heard presentations Thursday in behalf of church members who said that Bishop Melvin Wheatley Jr. had acted improperly in making the appointment.

headline: Research
abstract: Question One came in an April poll by Patrick Caddell, Jimmy Carter's pollster, who now works for William Brown, a candidate for governor of Ohio. Referring to Jerry Springer, a Brown rival for the Democratic nomination, the question asked:   As you may know, in 1974 (Mr. Springer), who had gotten married six months earlier, was arrested on a morals charge with three women in a hotel room.

headline: SOUTH DAKOTA EXPORTING SUSPECTS
abstract: Gov. William J. Janklow of South Dakota says he has carried out a threat to export criminal defendants to California.   Ninety-three persons accused of a variety of crimes, including forgery, burglary, indecent exposure and theft, were allowed to avoid prosecution in the last five years if they agreed to move to California, he said. Nobody turned down the offer.

headline: Coast Professor, Suspended Over His Sex Course, Resigns
abstract: A professor who gave course credit for homosexual and extramarital sex and admitted being ''romantically involved'' with students has resigned without explanation, a university spokesman says.   Prof. Barry Singer, 39 years old, informed officials at California State University, Long Beach, of his resignation May 28, two days after he was suspended pending a university investigation of his ''Psychology of Sex'' course.

headline: THE HOMOSEXUAL MARKET
abstract: Yes, there is a gay market; there is also a lesbian market despite the fact that the word ''lesbian'' did not appear in your article.  However, we are not ''recession proof.''

headline: WESTERN GOVERNORS JOIN BATTLE OVER EXTRADITIONS
abstract: In a modern-day version of get-out-oftown-before-sundown frontier justice, a verbal battle has erupted between South Dakota and California over the extradition of suspected criminals.   The battle was between Gov. William J. Janklow of South Dakota, who said he had allowed 93 suspected criminals to move to California to escape prosecution over the past five years, and Gov. Edmund G. Brown Jr. of California, who said that Governor Janklow was lying.   While the Governors exchanged words and hard feelings between the states grew, the man who spurred the controversy, Dennis Banks, the former leader of the American Indian Movement, remained free in California.   The latest round began June 3, when Mr. Janklow, a Republican, was quoted in a California newspaper saying that he had allowed 93 people facing felony charges ranging from burglary and forgery to picking pockets and indecent exposure to move to California and escape prosecution here. He was upset that California harbored Mr. Banks, whom Mr. Janklow prosecuted on riot and assault charges in 1975.

headline: No Headline
abstract: The article ''Tapping the Homosexual Market'' by Karen Stabiner (May 2) overstated the figure for the over-18 population of the United States, and thus in turn overstated the estimate of this country's homosexual population. The correct 1980 census figure for those over 18 is 162,751,000. The correct estimate of the homosexual population is 8 to 10 million.

headline: The Homosexual Market
abstract: Karen Stabiner's article ''Tapping the Homosexual Market'' (May 2) focuses on the more affluent segment of the gay market. But this segment of the market is not necessarily congruent with the out-of-thecloset gays, and certainly not with those who have fought and struggled for the application of the American Constitution to the gay community.

headline: CLUE FOUND ON HOMOSEXUALS' PRECANCER SYNDROME
abstract: Federal epidemiologists investigating a serious disorder of the body's immune system that has mostly afflicted male homosexuals reported new evidence yesterday suggesting that the outbreak is linked to an infectious agent.   ''We think the findings are important but they don't solve the problem,'' Dr. Harold W. Jaffe, one of the epidemiologists at the Centers for Disease Control in Atlanta, said in an interview. ''They do show pretty convincingly that this is not occurring as a random event among homosexual men.''

headline: FIGURE IN RICHMOND INQUIRY GETS 4 YEARS IN PRISON
abstract: A Brooklyn man who has charged entrapment by Federal agents investigating Representative Frederick W. Richmond was given a fouryear prison sentence yesterday for conspiracy to distribute cocaine.   The man, Joseph Marino, 29 years old, pleaded guilty May 5 to a single conspiracy count under an agreement in which the Government dropped three other charges involving distribution of three ounces of cocaine, worth $6,600.   Under the informal plea-bargaining agreement, Judge Thomas C. Platt of Federal Court in Brooklyn could have sentenced Mr. Marino to five years in prison and a $25,000 fine. The original charges carried a 15-year sentence and a fine on each count.

headline: HOW CONSERVATIVES VIEW U.S. POSTS
abstract: Bob Billings is a Christian evangelist who believes that rock music, sex education and homosexuality are bad and that we live in a ''corrupt, decadent society.''   ''But I've had to soft-pedal my views,'' says Mr. Billings, who took a job high in the hierarchy of the Department of Education last year. ''If I was on the outside, I could be more vocal.''   Nonetheless, Mr. Billings, the former director of Moral Majority and a graduate of Bob Jones University, is quietly pushing a social agenda within the Reagan Administration that re-flects his fundamentalist Christian views. ''I have not changed my principles,'' he says. ''I have changed my tactics.''

headline: SUSPECT SEIZED IN TWO MURDERS IN WALL ST. AREA
abstract: A man who was given a conditional discharge from prison last December was arrested yesterday and charged with the murder on Monday of two insurance executives in an office tower in Manhattan's financial district.   Detectives found the suspect, according to the police, through a job resume that had apparently fallen from his pocket as he struggled with his victims in a men's room in the office tower. The two men - one an office manager and the other an insurance underwriter for different companies - were shot and slashed to death Monday afternoon when they apparently resisted being robbed, the police said.   The arrested man was identified as Nathan Dodell, 28 years old, of 557 West 150th Street in Manhattan, who gave his occupation as temporary office worker.
