headline: PRIDE AND JOY AT HOMOSEXUAL PARADE
abstract: The annual Gay and Lesbian Pride March coursed through Manhattan yesterday in a buoyant celebration by tens of thousands of participants.   There were marching bands, baton twirlers, banners and balloons and aggregations of homosexual men, women, parents, teen-agers, artists, therapists, politicians and percussionists, representing an estimated 100 groups.   ''These are people enjoying their diverse interests - political, social, athletic, religious,'' said Richard May of the Christopher Street Liberation Day Committee, which organized the event. ''We can be people now, not objects.''

headline: After Dark Returning With Mid-August Issue
abstract: After Dark, a monthly magazine characterized as ''the chronicle of entertainment,'' is missing its June and July issues but will be out in mid-August with a combined August-September issue, according to Seth Cooper, a certified public accountant who is the new copublisher, treasurer and vice president, finance.   The issues were missed, he said, because of problems that arose when Lee Swanson and Louis Miele were trying to sell the publication. Mr. Cooper bought out Mr. Miele, and Mr. Swanson remains as copublisher and editor in chief.   The 14-year-old magazine has an unaudited circulation of between 60,000 and 70,000, Mr. Cooper said, noting that it had gotten a following in the homosexual community seven or eight years before any of the current homosexual magazines came on the market.

headline: HOUSE TO CHECK SEX REPORTS ON MEMBERS AND PAGES
abstract: The leadership of the House of Representatives today ordered an investigation into charges that some members of Congress had offered preferential treatment to teen-aged legislative pages in return for sexual favors.   The inquiry by the House Committee on Standards of Official Conduct was announced after the disclosure that the Justice Department had begun what was termed its own ''very preliminary'' investigation into one former page's statement that he had heard that pages had engaged in homosexual acts and drug use with House members.   The page was one of scores of teen-agers, often from families well-connected in the political and corporate world, who receive seasonal jobs to run office errands for the lawmakers and their staffs. He reportedly went to the Justice Department at the suggestion of House staff members after telling them of an encounter in which he said he had been sexually propositioned by a member of the House.

headline: EX-CONVICT RECEIVES SENTENCE OF 30 YEARS FOR ASSAULT IN BRONX
abstract: A former convict was sentenced yesterday to a maximum term of 30 years in prison for sodomy and attempted rape in a knifepoint attack on a 19-year-old college student in the Bronx last year.   Justice Alexander Chananau of State Supreme Court noted that the attack came six months after the defendant's release from prison on a term imposed for slashing another woman who had resisted his advances and that the defendant had attempted to assault a prosecutor on the day he was found guilty of the latest charges.   The defendant, Mark Dupree, 24, of 255 East 176th Street, in the Bronx, had been found guilty on June 7. He must serve at least 18 years before becoming eligible for parole, according to the Bronx District Attorney, Mario Merola.

headline: EX-PAGE REPORTED TO FAIL LIE TEST ON SEXUAL MISCONDUCT IN CONGRESS
abstract: Federal officials said today that a former Congressional page who was a primary source of allegations about homosexual activity on Capitol Hill had failed a polygraph examination administered by the Federal Bureau of Investigation.   The former page, Leroy Williams of Little Rock, Ark., acknowledged that he had failed the lie-detector test given to him Thursday but said that he stood by his story. After meeting today with investigators from the House ethics committee, Mr. Williams said that he had given them the names of three Congressmen with whom he had engaged in sexual acts.   The 18-year-old witness also said that he had supplied the name of a Senator for whom he had arranged an appointment with a male prostitute.

headline: HOUSE SET TO STUDY PAGES' ALLEGATIONS
abstract: Speaker of the House Thomas P. O'Neill Jr.  today rejected a call to appoint an independent prosecutor to investigate charges of sexual misconduct and drug use involving Capitol pages and members of Congress.   The Speaker characterized the charges as ''an affront to Congress, to the nation it serves and to basic human decency,'' but added, ''If the Congress cannot conduct an honest and comprehensive probe of these charges and punish those found guilty of these illegal acts, then the Congress has no right to make the laws that govern this nation.''   The allegations of homosexual relations and drug use were widely discussed as lawmakers began returning to the Capitol today from the July 4 recess. Few committees held meetings and no votes were scheduled, so most members of Congress stretched their vacations to Tuesday.

headline: ETHICS CHIEF VOWS A DILIGENT INQUIRY
abstract: The chairman of the House ethics committee today promised a thorough investigation into charges of drug use on Capitol Hill and homosexual acts between lawmakers and teen-age pages, but the panel's staff director was overheard saying that the matter could be wrapped up in two weeks.   Representative Louis Stokes, Democrat of Ohio, chairman of the panel, officially known as the Committee on Standards of Official Conduct, said that he and the panel's ranking Republican, Representative Floyd Spence of South Carolina, would appoint a special counsel with broad subpoena powers to conduct ''a thorough, professional investigation'' into ''all facets'' of the charges.   After a 90-minute closed committee meeting, Mr. Stokes declined to answer questions about remarks reporters overheard being made by John Swanner, the committee's staff director, just as the meeting was getting under way.   ''In two weeks time, we should be able to finish this up,'' Mr.  Swanner said.

headline: Immunology Breakdown Found in Hemophiliacs
abstract: A mysterious, often fatal breakdown of the body's immunity to disease, which was first detected in homosexual males, Haitian refugees and drug users, has been found in hemophiliacs and is increasing in frequency, health researchers reported today.   The national Centers for Disease Control reported three cases of pneumocystis carinii pneumonia in patients with hemophilia A but no other underlying disease. Researchers are concerned because the patients' immunological systems showed breakdowns ''strikingly similar'' to those found in the groups previously affected, the center said in its Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.

headline: BRITAIN WILL NOT PROSECUTE IN CASE OF PALACE INTRUDER
abstract: The intruder who surprised Queen Elizabeth in her bedroom at Buckingham Palace 10 days ago will not be prosecuted because he did not commit a criminal offense, the British authorities announced today.   The reason, they explained, is that in Britain trespassing is a violation of civil law, but not a crime.  The Government decision coincided with a second startling disclosure involving security at Buckingham Palace - an announcement that the police officer in charge of protecting the royal family had resigned after acknowledging that he had had a homosexual relationship with a male prostitute for a number of years. Public Outrage at the Incident   These new developments rekindled the fascination and outrage that have gripped a British public aghast that Michael Fagan, a 30-yearold unemployed laborer, was able to spend 10 minutes chatting with the Queen in her bedroom, unbeknown to security men.   The disclosure about Mr. Fagan came as he was charged in a London magistrates' court with having entered the palace on a previous occasion, on June 7, and stolen a bottle of wine, as well as with theft and assault arising from other, unrelated incidents.

headline: AT THE HEART OF THE ABSCAM DEBATE
abstract: Abdul Enterprises Ltd. may have looked like a gold mine to members of Congress who accepted money from associates of Arab sheiks. But when the Congressmen realized that they had stepped onto a land mine instead - that the sheiks were part of a sophisticated undercover operation -they raised a cry that is still echoing in Washington more than two years later.   Since Abscam first came to public attention in February 1980, the startling news that one Senator and six Congress-men had been tricked in a sting - and caught on videotape taking bribes - has raised questions about the uses, and the potential abuses, of undercover tactics. The subject has remained a topic of spirited debate, and not just in the courts, where the Congressmen's appeals are pending.   A Senate select committee was scheduled to begin hearings on Abscam last week and on the techniques that it involved. The aim is to assess how well the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Justice Department are monitoring such operations, to study their guidelines for approving clandestine investigations and to decide whether controlling legislation should be enacted. By December, when the committee's report is due, such thorny issues as entrapment, targeting and due process will have been examined fully.

headline: CONDUCT TO BE MONITORED IN CITY'S POLITICAL RACES
abstract: Thirty New Yorkers yesterday announced the formation of a new organization to monitor this year's political campaigns in the city.  The group seeks ''to discourage political campaigning that appeals to prejudice based on race, ethnicity, religious identity, national origin, gender or sexual orientation.''   Calling itself Conduct - Committee on Decent Unbiased Campaign Tactics - the group, which includes people of various racial, religious and political backgrounds, plans to receive complaints and ask candidates about them, publicizing responses.

headline: Ex-Congressman Quits Maryland G.O.P. Race
abstract: Former Representative Robert E.  Bauman, defeated in 1980 after acknowledging that he was an alcoholic with homosexual tendencies, today dropped out of the race to win back his House seat, saying he had been viciously attacked by an opponent and was tired of the demands of a political campaign.   The 45-year-old former Congressman said an aide to his Republican primary rival had implied that his acknowledgment of alcoholism and homosexual tendencies could become a campaign issue if he did not abandon the race.

headline: A DISEASE'S SPREAD PROVOKES ANXIETY
abstract: The persistence of a serious disease whose victims are primarily homosexual men has touched off anxiety among homosexuals in New York City, where nearly half of the nation's cases have been reported.   Doctors treating homosexuals say they are being flooded with telephone calls from old and new patients with minor complaints.  Clinics offering testing for the disease are oversubscribed. And homosexual men speak of great confusion over how to adjust their health habits to avoid the disease, which remains largely mysterious in its symptoms and causes.

headline: A PERSONAL ISSUE FOR 'NICK-PACK' HEAD
abstract: Terry Dolan, national chairman of the National Conservative Political Action Committee, has been privately warning leaders of the Republican new right about a forthcoming book that says he is a secret homosexual. He has sought, and apparently has received, the support of some key leaders of the conservative movement, including Richard A. Viguerie, a direct-mail fund raiser and the publisher of Conservative Digest.   Mr. Dolan, who is aware of the potential political fallout from the charge, said in an interview that he was not a homosexual, that he had never knowingly been to a homosexual bar and that he had never heard of his chief accuser, Richard Anderson, a young Federal employee who has signed an affidavit saying that he had a homosexual encounter with Mr. Dolan on Dec. 22, 1980.   The incident Mr. Anderson described is contained in the galley proofs of a forthcoming book, ''God's Bullies: Power Politics and Religious Tyranny,'' by Perry Deane Young, to be published later this year by Holt, Rinehart and Winston of New York. Mr. Young, a former newspaperman and a homosexual himself, was the co-author of the book, ''The David Kopay Story,'' an account of the professional football player's struggle with homosexuality.

headline: JUSTICE DEPT. READY TO HALT CONGRESS SEX INQUIRY
abstract: The Justice Department is winding down its investigation into allegations of sexual misconduct by members of Congress after finding no evidence to support charges made by former Congressional pages, according to department officials.   A related criminal investigation into possible narcotics violations by members of Congress and their staff members is continuing, the officials said.   The investigation of purported sexual misconduct began in July after several former pages, teen-agers who run errands in the House and Senate, said they had been involved in homosexual relations with members of Congress.

headline: Vote in Restroom Ruled Out
abstract: A vote by the city police commission on a grievance matter has been ruled invalid because it followed a discussion in a City Hall bathroom. The assistant city solicitor, John J. Rhodes, said the closed meeting was a clear violation of the Open Meeting Law. On Aug. 9, the three-member board had called the executive session on a grievance filed by a police lieutenant, and retired to a men's room.

headline: TEXAS BAN ON HOMOSEXUAL CONDUCT STRUCK DOWN
abstract: A Federal judge today struck down a Texas law prohibiting homosexual acts. Activists for homosexual rights said the ruling could make Texas the 26th state that no longer prohibits homosexual conduct.

headline: HOMOSEXUAL ATHLETIC MEET TO OPEN ON COAST
abstract: After three years of planning, a homosexual ''olympic-style athletic and human rights demonstration'' is to open in Kezar Stadium here next Saturday.   About 1,300 men and women will compete for nine days in 17 events, known as the Gay Games, ranging from track and field to billiards, bowling and weight-lifting. Men and women are to compete together on the track and swimming relay teams.

headline: Quotation of the Day
abstract: ''I have lied and I regret that. Words cannot express the remorse I feel.'' -Leroy Williams, a former Congressional page who alleged in March that he had had homosexual liaisons with members of Congress.  (1:1.)

headline: NEW YORK ISSUES NEW GUIDELINES ON ADOPTIONS FOR STATE'S AGENCY
abstract: New York has issued new guidelines for the State Adoption Service, stating that homosexuality, a criminal record or a history of alcohol or drug abuse need not necessarily be a bar to being an adoptive parent.   ''We're not lowering standards,'' said Terrance M. McGrath, a spokesman for the state's Department of Social Services. ''What we're doing is making sure that anybody who is not only eligible to adopt, but who would make a good parent for a child, is considered.''

headline: FORMER PAGE NOW ASSERTS HE LIED IN TELLING OF SEX WITH LAWMAKERS
abstract: Leroy Williams, the former Congressional page who said in March that he had had homosexual liaisons with lawmakers, said today that he had lied.   ''These allegations are not true,'' the 18-year-old Mr. Williams said at a news conference. ''I have lied and I regret that. Words cannot express the remorse I feel.''

headline: EX-PAGE SWEARS CHARGES WERE LIES
abstract: Leroy Williams, a former Congressional page, testified under oath today that he had never had homosexual relations with a member of Congress, thereby fully recanting an allegation he made earlier this year.   Appearing for more than three hours at a private session of the House ethics committee to make a deposition, Mr. Williams said he had lied when he said he had had homosexual relations with three Representatives and had also arranged a liaison between a male prostitute and a Senator.   ''Leroy Williams testified that his contrary statements to this committee's investigators, to the F.B.I. and to the media were false,'' said Representative Louis Stokes, Democrat of Ohio, who is chairman of the House Committee on Standards of Official Conduct, commonly known as the ethics committee. Had Recanted in Little Rock   Mr. Williams first said publicly on Friday that he had lied about the allegations, telling a news conference in Little Rock, Ark., ''Words cannot express the remorse I feel.''

headline: Former Page Says He Lied
abstract: Though the Justice Department's investigation of sexual misconduct on Capitol Hill has wound down, to concentrate instead on apparently more substantial charges of drug abuse, the House ethics committee's version was only beginning. Yesterday, it appeared to be just about over, as 18-year-old Leroy Williams, a former Congressional page whose allegations of homosexual liaisons with lawmakers prompted both inquiries - and a commission to review the page system besides - told the committee that he had lied.   Mr. Williams went public with his recantation in Little Rock, Ark., last week, after two committee investigators questioned him alone at a near-by state recreational area.

headline: PRESUMPTION OF GUILT
abstract: When an embittered young attention-seeker charged that members of Congress were engaging Congressional pages in homosexual acts, the sordid accusation led the television news broadcasts and was given important play in the press. A nervous House called for an investigation, the F.B.I. was brought in and eminent counsel was retained.   Last week, the accuser was faced with a prospect he had not foreseen: he would have to repeat his charge under oath, and if he failed to tell the truth, he would face perjury prosecution. At that point, the accuser called in the cameras and admitted that his charge of homosexual seduction was a lie.

headline: Quotation of the Day
abstract: ''Since the positions of the Government of the United States seriously deviate from the Camp David agreement, contradict it and could create a serious danger to Israel, its security and its future, the Government of Israel has resolved that on the basis of these positions it will not enter into any negotiations with any party.'' -The Israeli Cabinet. (A8:6.)

headline: THE POLITICAL ISSUE OF SEXUAL ORIENTATION
abstract: To the Editor:   In his Aug. 30 column, ''Presumption of Guilt,'' William Safire discusses a topic which rarely makes it into print at The Times. The topic is homosexuality.   Mr. Safire correctly states that homosexuality seems to be the current smear tactic being used against officeholders and others.  While his diagnosis of the problem is accurate, his prognosis bears some scrutiny.

headline: OF NEWS
abstract: The elements of the story, first reported by CBS News the evening of June 30, were undeniably sensational. Federal law-enforcement officials, CBS News said, were investigating allegations that several unidentified Congressman had engaged in homosexual activity with teen-age Congressional pages. Two former pages, interviewed on camera in silhouette, detailed their accusations.   Ten days later, one of the former pages, Leroy Williams, made his allegations before a Congressional subcommittee. But late last month, after Mr. Williams failed a polygraph, or lie-detector, test and law-enforcement officials were unable to corroborate any of his allegations, he recanted. Last week the Justice Department officially ended its inquiry, citing ''insufficient evidence.''   Even before the credibility of the allegations became a public issue, the question of how to treat the story was a subject of debate for news organizations that had been investigating longstanding rumors of homosexual activity on Capitol Hill. The broad issues included these:   - How does a news organization balance the public's right to know with the need to protect innocent people from unverified allegations?

headline: NO NEED FOR ADVOCATES
abstract: To the Editor:     In his Aug. 30 column, William Safire speaks of ''advocates of homosexuality.''

headline: Data Said to Show U.S. Spied On Homosexual Rights Units
abstract: The Federal Government routinely spied on organizations promoting homosexual rights and compiled voluminous lists of homosexuals in the 1950's, 1960's and early 1970's, according to documents from the Pentagon and the Federal Bureau of Investigation.   The documents, released under the Freedom of Information Act and obtained from a private source, show that considerable surveillance of homosexual rights organizations took place in San Francisco, which has a large homosexual population, but F.B.I. agents across the country were involved.

headline: BRIEFING
abstract: No Deadline for Ethics   The House Committee on Standards of Official Conduct would like to wrap up its investigation of charges of sexual misconduct and illegal drug use by members of Congress and Capitol Hill pages by Oct. 8, the day Congress is scheduled to adjourn, to clear the political air before the November elections.   However, Representative Louis Stokes, the Ohio Democrat who is chairman of the ethics panel, has confided to some that the committee is a little nervous about concluding its own investigation before a Federal grand jury presents its findings. The ethics panel does not want to be embarrassed should the grand jury turn up something its own investigators missed.   The House investigation got off to a sensational start earlier this year when a former Congressional page, Leroy Williams of Little Rock, Ark., told the Federal Bureau of Investigation that some senators and representatives had engaged in homosexual acts with pages. Mr.  Williams later admitted making up the story, but not until after the committee had retained Joseph A. Califano Jr. as its special counsel and Gerald T. McQueen, a New York City police detective, as its chief investigator.

headline: Former Congressman Concedes in Maryland
abstract: Former Representative Robert E. Bauman announced Friday that he would not challenge the results of the Republican primary in Maryland's First Congressional District despite voting machine problems in one county.   Mr. Bauman, who lost his House seat in 1980 after disclosing that he suffered from alcoholism and ''homosexual tendencies,'' said the tally was not close enough to make a challenge worthwhile, even with the machine malfunctions in Queen Anne's County.

headline:
NEW JERSEY GUIDE;
F.Y.I., IT'S P.D.Q.
abstract:
''The Intimate P.D.Q. Bach,'' which makes a mockery of serious music to the delight of even its most stodgy devotees, will be presented Friday at 8 P.M. at the John Harms Englewood Plaza for the Performing Arts in Englewood.

Prof. Peter Schickele discovered P.D.Q. (1807-1742), a very forgotten son of Johann Sebastian Bach, 16 years ago. Friday's program will include the ''Goldbrick Variations'' and ''Hansel and Gretel and Ted and Alice,'' an opera in one unnatural act that features a longtime associate of Professor Schickele's, John Ferrante, a bargain-counter tenor.

This ''new second edition'' of ''Intimate P.D.Q. Bach'' will also include, according to a spokesman for the John Harms center (who crossed his heart), ''comments on the life and times of P.D.Q. Bach, fully illustrated by Professor Schickele's collection of rare slides, manuscripts and other memorabilia.''

The professor will also play the piano, the bassoon and the Baroque Calliope.  The Baroque Calliope?  P.D.Q. is part of the John Harms Great Entertainer Series. Other performances in the series are the Norman Luboff Choir, Nov. 23 at 3 P.M.; Marian McPartland, jazz pianist, March 26 at 8 P.M., and the Joffrey II Dancers, May 7 at 8 P.M.

headline: Catholic Group Provokes Debate on Homosexuals
abstract: A proposal by a group of priests, nuns and lay leaders to open Roman Catholic Church doors to practicing homosexuals has ignited renewed debate of the Church's longstanding disapproval of homosexual behavior.   The group, formed to deal with homosexual issues, issued a report calling for the open acceptance of homosexuals as members of the Church and as teachers, as well as to expand education and promote Catholic acceptance of homosexuality into every aspect of church life. The group also suggests that 30 percent of the Catholic clergy today may be homosexually oriented.

headline: BRIEFING
abstract: Gain for Homosexuals   I n 1977, then Vice President Walter F. Mondale was booed off the stage at a Democratic fund-raising event in San Francisco for refusing to address the subject of homosexual rights. Thereafter, homosexual activists complained that Mr. Mondale repeatedly refused their requests to meet at the White House to discuss the issue.   It is no wonder, then, that many of these same activists are applauding Mr. Mondale's decision to appear as the keynote speaker at a fund-raising dinner in New York Wednesday night sponsored by the Washington-based Human Rights Campaign Fund, a political action committee that is raising money for candidates who support homosexual rights legislation. The New York dinner is one of several being held around the country.

headline: Wild Jails, Closed Minds
abstract: A series of articles in The Washington Post this week about the jail in nearby Prince George's County, Md., inspires fascination, disgust and a message for political leaders everywhere. The articles document that rape has become a routine part of prison life. Though the act is homosexual, it has become an expression of manhood in the perverse subculture that flourishes beyond the view of inattentive or frightened guards.

headline: MONDALE TELLS HOMOSEXUAL GROUP REAGAN RECORD IS BIASED ON RIGHTS
abstract: Former Vice President Walter F. Mondale appealed to more than 1,000 homosexual rights activists and their supporters last night to join the Democratic Party in fighting what he called the ''irrational discrimination'' of the Reagan Adminstration.   Mr. Mondale made his remarks at a dinner at the Waldorf-Astoria Hotel intended to raise funds for the Human Rights Campaign Fund, a federally registered political action committee seeking to influence the outcome of several Congressional races this fall. Mr. Mondale, regarded as a leading contender for the Democratic Presidential nomination in 1984, accused the Reagan Administration of weakening the nation's commitment to human rights.   ''Of all the principles the Reagan Administration is weakening, the most important in the long run may well be this country's commitment to universal human rights,'' said Mr. Mondale in a defense of the Carter Administration's rights record.

headline: DECRIMINALIZING HEROIN
abstract: It is time to raise a new cry for the decriminalization of heroin and other drugs such as cocaine and marijuana.  American courts and prisons are tremendously overworked. We can no longer afford the burden placed upon them by the enforcement of drug laws. We should recognize the futility of attempting to cure society's drug problems through the criminal justice system and, instead, make drugs that are now illegal available to adults who want them. This approach appears to be the least expensive and best way of substantially reducing courts' work loads, and, as a bonus, making a significant dent in the rate of street crime.

headline: Judge Rules Army Must Let Homosexual Continue Duty
abstract: A Federal judge has ruled that a 34-yearold career soldier cannot be barred from re-enlistment simply because he is an avowed homosexual.

headline: THE MIDEAST ROOTS OF THE ISRAELI MAJORITY
abstract: To the Editor:    In accusing you of misunderstanding history and misreading the facts, M. T. Mehdi (letter Oct. 3) himself distorts history and perverts the facts.   Israelis, he says, are Europeans and Americans, without as much as alluding to the large number of Sephardim, mostly Arab Jews, who for centuries, if not millennia, had lived in the so-called Arab countries of the Middle East.

headline: WILD JAILS AND A MISUNDERSTOOD OFFENSE
abstract: To the Editor:    Your Sept. 30 editorial ''Wild Jails, Closed Minds'' is a disgraceful example of an archaic and destructive attitude toward the homosexual community in particular and toward the affirmation of human rights at large.    Homosexuality is not an act in and of itself.

headline: Marchers Protest Raid on 43d St. Bar
abstract: Several hundred demonstrators marched through the Times Square area last night to protest what they called ''police brutality'' aimed at homosexual patrons of a bar on 43d Street east of Eighth Avenue.   ''Hey, hey, ho, ho, police brutality has got to go,'' members of the crowd chanted as they marched from Times Square south on Broadway, then west one block on 42d Street, one block north on Eighth Avenue and then east on 43d Street back to Times Square.

headline: Army Asks Right to Bar Homosexual Sergeant
abstract: The Army, worried that a homosexual sergeant might have sexual relations with other soldiers, has gone back to Federal court to try to prevent him from re-enlisting.   A lawyer for the 14-year Army veteran, Sgt. Perry Watkins, filed a countermotion Monday asking the judge to allow his client to reenlist for six years when his tour expires on Oct. 25.

headline: PEANUTS
abstract:
After Columbia Pictures discovered that David Begelman had embezzled $60,000, he was kept on by the board at a handsome annual stipend. Reading the story in David McClintick's ''Indecent Exposure,'' the world seems shocked, surprised; there is moralistic jumping up and down, yelling and screaming. What's the big deal, numbers-wise (as the M.B.A.'s say)?

What'd Begelman cost his company by comparison with John Bunting of the First National Bank of Pennsylvania? Or Harding Lawrence of Braniff Airlines? Or the grand-designers at Addressograph-Multigraph? Or the still incumbent top managers at Chase Manhattan and the Continental Illinois National Bank? Or Amax? Or Sohio?

headline: Judge Rules Homosexual Can Re-enlist in Army
abstract: The Army must let a sergeant who acknowledges he is a homosexual re-enlist despite his refusal to answer questions about his future sexual activity, Federal District Judge Barbara Rothstein has ruled.   James Lobsenz, the lawyer for Sgt. Perry Watkins, said he expected the Army to appeal.

headline: MOZAMBIQUE KEEPS TO MARXIST ROUTE
abstract: Although Mozambique appears to be trying to improve relations with the West, there has been no matching domestic move to deviate from Marxist theory.   While some foreign diplomats attribute Mozambique's poor economic performance to unsuccessful socialist ventures, the ruling Mozambique Liberation Front has made what one diplomat called ''only a pious bow'' in the direction of looser economic controls to provide greater incentives. Instead, recently published guidelines for next year's party congress call for ''the reinforcement of the controlling position of our Marxist-Leninist party.''   The guidelines are framed in what are called the ''eight theses'' up for discussion at the fourth party congress of the Mozambique Liberation Front, known as Frelimo. The first of these says: ''Our conquests result from the socialist nature of our revolution. Only the people's struggle under the direction of Frelimo can defend, consolidate and widen them.''

headline: DEATH BENEFIT VOTED FOR HOMOSEXUAL'S LOVER
abstract: The homosexual lover and business partner of an assassinated Supervisor, Harvey Milk, should receive a portion of survivor's death benefits, according to a ruling in this city with a large homosexual population.   The death benefits ruling, passed Tuesday by the San Francisco Retirement Board on a vote of 3 to 1, marked the first time such benefits were given to the survivor of a homosexual relationship, according to board records.   Meanwhile, a committee of the Board of Supervisors on Tuesday proposed granting the same city employee benefits to homosexual couples and unmarried heterosexuals as it does to married couples.

headline: London Inquiry Clears Queen's Ex-Bodyguard
abstract: Queen Elizabeth's former police bodyguard was cleared today of breaching Buckingham Palace security while he lived a secret double life as a homosexual having affairs with male prostitutes.   Michael Trestrail, 51 years old, quit in disgrace last July in a scandal over palace security brought to light by the discovery of an intruder who crept into the royal bedchamber at night and chatted with the Queen.

headline: COUPLE LAW ASKED FOR SAN FRANCISCO
abstract: A proposed ordinance supported by San Francisco's large homosexual community would create a new class of ''domestic partners,'' allowing live-in lovers to be covered by the city's employee insurance programs.   The measure, already passed by a vote of 8 to 3 in its first reading, would make San Francisco the first city to recognize unmarried domestic partners as having rights now reserved for husbands and wives.   The proposal, offered by the Board of Supervisors' only member who has declared that he is homosexual, will come up for final passage Monday. Mayor Dianne Feinstein has not taken a public position on the measure, but, given its present support on the board, it could be passed over her veto.

headline: ARTIFICIAL HEART IMPLANT IS BEGUN IN SALT LAKE
abstract: A retired Seattle dentist suffering from inoperable heart disease underwent surgery late tonight for what was to be the first transplant of a permanent artificial heart.   Barney Clark, 61 years old, had been scheduled receive the fistsized polyurethane device Thursday morning at the Utah Medical Center, but his rapidly deteriorating condition led doctors to begin an emergency operation at 10:30 P.M. The operation by a team of University of Utah doctors was expected to last three to four hours.   Dr. Clark suffered from cardiomyopathy, a degenerate disease of the heart muscle. He was among 10 prospective recipients of the revolutionary device, called the Jarvik-7, for Dr. Robert Jarvik of the university's Artificial Organs Division, who developed the device.

headline: JURY GIVEN LESSON IN HOLLYWOOD LIFE
abstract: Eight women and four men boarded vans this week and were handed a document titled: ''Jury Viewing Itinerary, Night 1, Yolanda Washington and Judy Miller.''   For almost five hours, they were driven through a neon-lit Hollywood devoid of film stars or glamour - a city of homosexual street hustlers, female prostitutes and runaways. Then they were driven past Forest Lawn Cemetery and a hillside where the body of Miss Washington was found Oct. 17, 1977. Charged in 10 Murders   They were jurors in one of the longest criminal trials in California history. The defendant, Angelo Buono, a 47-year-old former auto upholsterer, is charged with murdering 10 young women in a case detectives refer to as the Hillside strangler killings.

headline: New Hepatitis Vaccine Effective for 2 Groups
abstract: A newly developed hepatitis vaccine is effective for up to five years against a type of hepatitis that annually afflicts 200,000 Americans, mainly hospital employees, homosexual men and drug addicts, a doctor reported today.   Dr. Cladd E. Stevens of the New York Blood Center reported in The New England Journal of Medecine that the vaccine, called Heptavax-B, was the first to be effective for two high-risk groups of people: those who come in contact with contaminated needles or blood and those to whom the virus is transmitted sexually.

headline: INFANT WHO RECEIVED TRANSFUSION DIES OF IMMUNE DEFICIENCY ILLNESS
abstract: The Centers for Disease Control in Atlanta reported yesterday that an infant who had received blood transfusions developed a serious immune-deficiency disease that has principally afflicted homosexuals.    The child had received multiple transfusions of blood and blood products, including a transfusion from a man who later proved to have acquired immune deficiency syndrome, called AIDS, The disorder has been linked primarily to homosexual men. The child died at the age of 20 months from infections related to the immune deficiency.

headline: PARTNERSHIP LAW VETOED ON COAST
abstract: Mayor Dianne Feinstein today vetoed a San Francisco city ordinance that would have extended to live-in lovers, including homosexuals, the health insurance benefits that now go to husbands and wives of city employees.   The San Francisco Roman Catholic Archdiocese issued a statement praising the veto as ''a courageous act'' in protection of family life, but Mayor Feinstein explained her veto in different terms.   ''I go out all over the world and defend this city,'' said the Mayor, whose election in 1979 was achieved with heavy support of the homosexual population, which has been estimated to be 15 percent. ''I must believe in what I am defending. I would love to go out and defend a document for the changing life styles we have in our city.  This is not that document.''

headline: CORRECTIONS
abstract: An article yesterday incorrectly stated the outcome of a blood transfusion received by an infant from an adult who was later diagnosed as having acquired immune deficiency syndrome. The infant developed a severe immune deficiency but is still alive.

headline: LEGAL MARIJUANA: BAD IDEA GETTING WORSE
abstract: To the Editor:     Peter Passell argues in his Nov. 29 Editorial Notebook article for ''regulation and taxation'' of marijuana. Legalization would, he writes, produce tax revenues of up to $2 billion a year and provide uncontaminated and even ''low tar'' pot.$ Many readers may have wondered, ''Why not?'' There are answers.  Before getting to them, however, several facts need to be understood. In the last decade, the catalogue of negative health effects of marijuana -once thought to be a ''harmless giggle'' - has grown alarmingly, to include serious damage to the lungs, brain and reproductive organs as well as a wide range of behavioral toxicities whose ultimate effects range from decreased school and work performance to highway fatalities.   Along with the growing awareness of these serious health effects, marijuana use among the young, which had risen relentlessly for two decades, peaked in 1978 and now appears to be declining. Public support for legalization and even the less extreme ''decriminalization'' also peaked in 1978. No state has decriminalized marijuana possession since 1978.

headline: Child Case Moves Red Cross To Study Blood Donor Policy
abstract: The American Red Cross will review its policy for selecting blood donors following reports that a 20-month-old baby in San Francisco may have gotten an often-fatal immune deficiency from a donor, the group's director says.   However, because Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome may have a long incubation period, ''changes in donor selection or transfusion practices may not have an immediate effect on the number of new cases reported,'' Dr. Alfred Katz of Washington said in a story published here Saturday.   The syndrome, found largely among male homosexuals and drug abusers, has been found in as many as 20 children, said Dr. James Oleske of New Jersey Hospital and St. Michael's Medical Center in Newark.

headline: HOUSE UNIT FINDS NO TRUTH IN SEX ALLEGATIONS
abstract: A House ethics panel that has been investigating allegations of homosexuality and sexual misconduct by members of Congress and its pages issued an interim report today concluding that ''virtually every one'' of the charges was unfounded.    Joseph A. Califano Jr., special counsel to the House Committee on Standards of Official Conduct, said in issuing the report that the inquiry was continuing to look into a few further charges of sexual misconduct. He also said that the panel was only beginning to examine other allegations regarding the use and distribution of drugs by members of Congress and employees.

headline: Photo in Patz Case Released by Police
abstract: A photograph of a boy possibly resembling Etan Patz, who disappeared more than three years ago in lower Manhattan, was released yesterday by the Police Department. The photograph was found this month in a house in Wareham, Mass., that the authorities said had been used by a homosexual organization.

headline: HOMOSEXUAL ADOPTING A SON
abstract: A judge has granted a 29-year-old homosexual permission to adopt his teen-age foster son.  ''Oh, God, I'm happy,'' David Frater said in a telephone interview Tuesday following the hearing that gave him adoption rights to Kevin Frater, 17 years old. ''This is the greatest Christmas present ever.''

headline: GROUP PROMOTING MAN-BOY LOVE IS THE FOCUS OF POLICE INQUIRY
abstract: Four years ago this month, after two dozen men were indicted for sex crimes in the nearby town of Revere, a conference was held downtown at the Community Church of Boston. About 30 men stayed on to talk of the difficult issue discussed at the conference, and they decided to form an organization to promote understanding of their kind of love and to seek a change in the law.   Thus, in the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, where many of the laws on sexual conduct date from the Puritan period, was born the most provocative name of any homosexual organization in the United States: the North American Man-Boy Love Association, dedicated to the proposition that state laws establishing a sexual age of consent should be repealed.   ''We had no idea where it would go,'' says David Thorstad, 41 years old, a freelance editor in New York, one of the founders of the group, known by its acronym Nambla. For the next several years it produced literature and held conferences in Boston, New York, Philadelphia and Baltimore, promoting the legitimacy of emotional and sexual love between adult men and young boys and arguing that the state laws that made such relationships illegal should be repealed.

headline: BRITISH DRAMA
abstract: The American premiere of ''Another Country'' by Julian Mitchell will take place at 8 P.M. Thursday, at the Long Wharf Theater in New Haven. A drama about the British public school system in the 1930's, it won the Best Play award from the Society of West End Theaters in England last summer, and it is currently running at the Queen's Theater in London.   With Peter MacNichols and Peter Gallagher in the leading roles, ''Another Country'' examines the upper-class British schools that produced future government leaders. It is based on the actual story of Guy Burgess, who attended such a school and later, as an adult in government service, defected to the Soviet Union. The incident was covered widely in the press some years ago, exploiting homosexual aspects of the case which are dealt with in the Long Wharf production.

headline: Kidnap Suspect Brought to Jersey
abstract: A man accused of kidnapping a 13-year-old New Jersey boy and taking him to a cottage in Massachusetts used by a homosexual organization was extradited to New Jersey from Vermont today.   The man, Hugh Hamill, 22 years old, of Chichester, N.Y., will be arraigned at 11 A.M. Wednesday in Superior Court in Monmouth County.

headline: DISEASE STIRS FEAR ON BLOOD SUPPLY
abstract: Health officials trying to find ways to stop a deadly immune deficiency say they are afraid that whatever causes the mysterious illness might contaminate supplies of blood for transfusions.   Public health officials and blood experts met here Tuesday at the national Centers for Disease Control to discuss possible ways to curb the spread of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome, which robs the body of its ability to fight off deadly infections.   The syndrome has fatal consequences in 40 percent of cases, and has been identified in four primary groups: homosexual males, people who use drugs intravenously, Haitian immigrants and hemophiliacs. The disorder has become the second leading cause of death among hemophiliacs.

headline: FEDERAL GRAND JURY INVESTIGATING CONGRESSMEN IN CAPITOL HILL DRUG USE CASE
abstract: A Federal grand jury is investigating allegations that five or six members of the House of Representatives have been using marijuana or cocaine, according to senior lawenforcement officials familiar with the inquiry.   The sources said investigators believed that Congressional staff aides and pages were also involved in drug use and distribution but that the authorities did not yet know the extent of it. The inquiry into drug use on Capitol Hill began last summer, after two former pages made public assertions of homosexuality, sexual misconduct and drug use in Congress.   One of those under investigation, law-enforcement officials said, is former Representative Barry M. Goldwater Jr. of California, a seven-term Representative who gave up his House seat to run for the Senate and then lost in the primary election last year. Officials said that several young women friends of Mr. Goldwater had assisted in the inquiry and that one of them had since gone into the Federal Witness Protection Program.

headline: HOMOSEXUAL VIEWS ADOPTION APPROVAL AS VICTORY
abstract: Two years ago, when he was 27 years old, David Frater thought that it was time he enjoyed the satisfactions that he felt fatherhood would bring.   He decided on adoption, and a long fight ended successfully when he became the adoptive father of a 17-year-old boy. He also established something of a legal precedent. Mr. Frater is a homosexual.   His adoption of the boy, Kevin, who has taken Mr. Frater's name, is believed by some social service and homosexual organizations to represent the first legal adoption by an acknowledged homosexual. The move was approved last month by Judge George Grover of Superior Court, who said he had considered Mr. Frater's sexual orientation as he would any number of factors in a parent-child relationship.

headline: The Civil Rights of Police
abstract: To the Editor:     Your Jan. 12 editorial opinion expressed in ''Ethics and Off-Duty Police'' reflects a surprisingly shallow viewpoint that is completely antithetical to the well-established civil rights consciousness of The Times.   he Times has unflinchingly championed the constitutional rights of even the vilest of criminals, yet with executioner-like finality the editorial prejudges ''accused'' police officers and casually obviates the inherent right of other officers to demonstrate support of peers merely charged with misconduct but not yet found guilty. In so doing, The Times perverts our fundamental system of justice, the cornerstone of which is the presumption of innocence, and also invokes an insidious double standard.

headline: HEMOPHILIAC GROUP WANTS BAR TO BLOOD LINKED TO SYNDROME
abstract: A ban on accepting blood donations that may reach hemophiliacs from those likely to be carriers of a disease that cripples the body's immune system has been recommended by the Medical and Scientific Advisory Council of the National Hemophilia Foundation.   The disease, acquired immune deficiency syndrome, or AIDS, is a recently identified disorder of unknown cause and high mortality.

headline: Ex-Convict Guilty in Slayings
abstract: An ex-convict was found guilty last night of murder in the slayings of two Wall Street executives. The defendant, Nathan Dodell, 28 years old, of Manhattan, was convicted in State Supreme Court in Manhattan in the June deaths of Michael Bonseiro, 32, of East Meadow, L.I., and Thomas Semple, 36, of Bloomfield, N.J. He was accused of killing the men during a robbery attempt in a men's room at 127 John Street. His job resume was found at the scene.

headline: Snowstorm Hits South, Causing Traffic Mishaps Accidents As Storm Moves North
abstract: A storm with freezing rain and snow fanned north from the South yesterday, making travel hazardous from New Mexico to West Virginia.   Power was knocked out for thousands in the Southeast and numerous traffic accidents were reported, including one in Alabama that slightly injured the singer Anita Bryant.

headline: AGAINST PUERTO RICAN STATEHOOD
abstract:
The resurgence of F.A.L.N. violence in New York City gives rise once again to the question of what Washington's policy should be toward Puerto Rico.

Acts of pro-independence terrorism, like those of the Fuerzas Armadas de Liberacion Nacional (Armed Forces of National Liberation) are more likely to produce, in Washington, further frustration than clear policy toward the island

A decade ago, Puerto Rico's rapidly expanding economy and solid democratic institutions were a source of pride to Washington's policy makers. Today, Puerto Rico is a headache. There is awareness that the economic and political situation there is deteriorating dangerously, that something must be done before it degenerates into another Caribbean crisis. But what?

headline: AIDS A NEW DISEASE'S DEADLY ODYSSEY
abstract: Robin Marantz Henig is the author of ''Your Premature Baby,'' to be published in the spring.   Medical detectives are calling it the century's most virulent epidemic. It is as relentless as leukemia, as contagious as hepatitis, and its cause has eluded researchers for more than two years. Acquired immune deficiency syndrome, or AIDS, was first seen in homosexual men - particularly those who were promiscuous - but it has now struck so many different groups that its course cannot be predicted.   And despite a massive nationwide microbe hunt involving hundreds of investigators and millions of dollars, scientists simply cannot catch up with it. ''We're always a few steps behind,'' says Dr. William W.  Darrow, a research sociologist with the Centers for Disease Control (C.D.C.) in Atlanta, ''and that makes us very, very concerned. The disease could be anywhere now.''

headline: 2 Doctors in U.S. Agency Back Hepatitis B Vaccine
abstract: A new hepatitis B vaccine made from blood plasma, which it is feared may contain an agent of the often-deadly acquired immune deficiency syndrome, or AIDS, is safe and highly effective, two physicians from the Food and Drug Administration say.   Some health-care workers have refused to be vaccinated because some of the plasma is obtained from hepatitis B-positive male homosexuals, the primary victims of AIDS disease.

headline: City Council to Hold 7 Meetings This Week
abstract: The City Council and its committees have scheduled seven meetings this week. They are: TUESDAY - The Committee on General Welfare considers a bill to prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, City Hall, 9 A.M.   WEDNESDAY - The Committee on Housing and Buildings considers a report by the Buildings Department on the installation of sprinklers and standpipes, City Hall, 10 A.M.   The Committee on Civil Service and Labor questions city and union officials on the development and administration of Civil Service examinations, 250 Broadway, 23d floor, noon.   The Committee on Transportation considers bills and resolutions on the use, registration and sale of bicycles, City Hall, 1:30 P.M.  THURSDAY - The full Council meets, City Hall, 1:30 P.M.  FRIDAY - The Committee on Governmental Operations considers realestate assessment procedures, City Hall, 10 A.M.  The Committee on Parks, Recreation and Cultural Affairs considers procedures for leasing park property and other matters, 250 Broadway, 23d floor, 1:30 P.M.

headline: BILL ON HOMOSEXUAL RIGHTS SUFFERS SETBACK IN COUNCIL
abstract: After more than 14 hours of testimony interrupted by both applause and jeers, a City Council committee defeated the homosexual rights bill early today, while angry spectators chanted ''justice, justice.''   Proponents promptly pressed plans to appeal to the full Council.  A few minutes after midnight, the Council's General Welfare Committee voted 6 to 3 against the bill, which would amend the city's human rights law to add ''sexual orientation'' to the criteria that cannot be used to justify discrimination in hiring, housing and public accommodations.   The criteria specified now are race, religion, sex, age and physical handicap.

headline: Plans Set to Move Sexual Rights Bill
abstract: City Council President Carol Bellamy said yesterday that she would move to have a homosexual rights bill discharged from the Council's General Welfare Committee as soon as Mayor Koch returned from a trip to Israel. He starts on the trip today.

headline: State High Court Kills Sexual Loitering Law
abstract: The State Court of Appeals today struck down a state law preventing the soliciting of another consenting adult for ''deviate'' sexual acts.

headline: A Possible Clue In AIDS Disease?
abstract: When scores of monkeys mysteriously sicken and die in a laboratory, it's sad for the monkeys and bad for researchers. But when the animal epidemic resembles a sometimes deadly human disease, ''acquired immune deficiency syndrome'' (AIDS), a tool for treatment may be at hand.
